title: Nowcasting Economic Activity in Afghanistan
abstract: Sound economic policy formulation requires high frequency economic activity data. This is particularly challenging in low-income, fragile, and conflict-affected states, such as Afghanistan, where quarterly GDP data is unavailable and annual GDP figures are published with considerable delays. This paper utilizes an innovative approach for estimating quarterly economic activity under these constraints, facilitating timely economic assessments in Afghanistan. Quarterly GDP data are interpolated from annual figures, utilizing money supply as a proxy indicator of economic activities due to Afghanistan’s predominately cash-based economy. By leveraging machine learning, traditional (macroeconomic), non-traditional (satellite) data, the approach provides real-time insights of the underlying direction of the Afghan economy at relatively high frequency and with partial information.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Afghanistan, a low-income, fragile, conflict-affected emerging economy, using money supply and satellite data to nowcast its activity. Its link to traded markets is weak.

title: Alternative Trade Corridors of the GCC
abstract: We provide the first quantitative general-equilibrium assessment of the trade and welfare effects of the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), a proposed rail-to-sea trade route through the Arabian Peninsula. We translate changes in transit times and transportation cost into bilateral trade costs and use them to inform a structural gravity counterfactual for over 200 countries and territories. We estimate that the declines in trade costs from IMEC would be modest, averaging 3.6 percent among affected pairs. Our results indicate that IMEC would benefit the GCC countries and Jordan most, with these countries gaining from the enhanced overland connectivity and more direct access to trade partners in Europe, North America, and North Africa. Upper- and lower-bound scenarios highlight the nonlinear role of relative rail and sea freight rates and the value of time in determining the corridor’s effectiveness, while additional sensitivity exercises show that transit delays can substantially reduce route adoption and the resulting gains.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the trade and welfare effects of the India-Middle East-Europe corridor, with gains concentrated in the GCC countries and Jordan, which are emerging or developing economies, though it also covers over 200 countries.

title: Treasury Issuance and Dealer Balance Sheets
abstract: Jonathan Glicoes, Lubomir Petrasek , Zack Saravay , and Mary Tian Primary dealers play an important role as intermediaries in Treasury securities and repo markets, and demand for their intermediation rises on issuance dates. Recent increases in Treasury issuance have raised questions about dealers' capacity to meet this increased demand.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US Treasury issuance and primary dealer balance sheets in the US Treasury and repo markets, which is a US advanced-economy focus.

title: When and for Whom Does the Sovereign-Bank Nexus Matter? Evidence from Post-Crisis Europe
abstract: Charlotte Hoopes, Pinar Uysal , and Ilknur Zer We study whether sovereign risk continues to affect banks a decade after Europe began reshaping its financial architecture. Combining daily bank and sovereign credit default swap spreads with supervisory data on banks' domestic sovereign portfolios, we show that the sovereign-bank relationship remains economically meaningful but is highly conditional. Banks with larger sovereign holdings respond more sharply to home-sovereign risk, and this amplification is substantially stronger for mark-to-market than amortized-cost exposures, consistent with more immediate recognition of valuation losses. Sovereign-to-bank transmission is stronger for less-capitalized, wholesale-funded, and peripheral banks, during periods of elevated market uncertainty, and when the home sovereign has less fiscal capacity. The policy reforms aimed at weakening the sovereignbank relationship only managed to reduce the extent of the link, but not eliminate it.
focus_rationale: The paper studies sovereign-bank linkages in Europe using bank and sovereign CDS spreads and supervisory data on domestic sovereign holdings, with peripheral euro area banks among the cases examined. The sample is advanced European economies.

title: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
abstract: Aditya Aladangady , Ricardo Duque Gabriel , and Carlo Wix We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely track traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level, capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level, and reproducing the impulse response of official consumption measures to identified monetary policy shocks. We then use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find suggestive evidence that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.
focus_rationale: The paper builds a US county-level consumption dataset from Fed Y-14M credit card data and studies US monetary policy transmission to consumption across the income distribution.

title: The effects of geopolitical risk on sovereign debt holders in the euro area
abstract: We use confidential granular data on euro area sovereign bond holdings to examine the heterogeneous behavior of investor types in response to country-specific geopolitical risk shocks. By distinguishing investor categories and accounting for their bond holding dynamics over time, we provide an empirical assessment of how different bond holders react to geopolitics. The analysis employs country-level geopolitical risk indices of the country of sovereign bonds, and applies local projection methods to estimate the dynamic responses of various investor groups to geopolitical risk shocks. In the case of high-debt euro area countries, i.e. Italy, France, Spain, and Belgium, we examine how geopolitical risks may trigger shifts in investor behavior that, in turn, could pose risks to fiscal sustainability.
focus_rationale: The paper studies euro area sovereign bond holdings and geopolitical risk shocks in Italy, France, Spain and Belgium, all advanced economies. It examines investor behaviour that bears on sovereign debt markets and fiscal sustainability.

title: Global Pension Reform Database 1952 – 2025
abstract: This paper introduces the Global Pension Reform Database (GPRD), the first dataset to provide systematic coverage of pension reforms across 142 advanced, emerging, and developing economies from 1952 to 2025. Leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) through a ring-fenced, locally hosted large language model (LLM), we extract and classify more than 4,000 pension reform episodes from the Economist Intelligence Unit and the U.S. Social Security Administration by type, timing, status, and generosity, enabling consistent cross-country and historical analysis. Stylized facts show that pension reform has shifted from an advanced-economy phenomenon to a global and recurring policy tool, often clustered around fiscal and macroeconomic crises. An empirical application demonstrates its analytical potential: in non-advanced economies, implemented pension reforms are associated with statistically significant and persistent declines in the public debt-to-GDP ratio, suggesting that such reforms can contribute to sustained fiscal consolidation.
focus_rationale: The database covers 142 advanced, emerging and developing economies globally, so it has no single market focus. Its fiscal consolidation finding for non-advanced economies links it to sovereign debt dynamics.

title: Are European Firms Financially Constrained?
abstract: We examine if European firms face binding financial constraints that explain Europe’s persistent scale-up gap. Using corporate tax changes as exogenous shocks and a "debt test", we analyze 7 million predominantly private firms across 20 euro area countries (2000–2022). A higher corporate tax rate increases the value of interest deductibility and, absent frictions, induces firms to increase leverage. We find that firms generally increase leverage after tax hikes, indicating constraints are not broadly binding. However, young firms and those in innovation-intensive industries show weaker responses. Among innovative firms, constraints vary: young firms appear unconstrained, while small, mature ones face binding constraints. Our findings suggest that financing frictions in Europe are concentrated among specific firm types at particular development stages, indicating that they are important at the critical scale-up stage.
focus_rationale: The paper studies firms across 20 euro area countries, all advanced economies, so it is DM.

title: A Global DSGE Model for Oil-Dependent Economies
abstract: This paper develops a global DSGE model linking oil-dependent economies to the systemic economies, and applies it to the GCC countries. The model features a range of nominal and real rigidities, extensive macrofinancial linkages, and diverse spillover transmission channels. Its modular structure also encompasses common features of oil-dependent economies, including a state-owned oil company, a capital intensive oil extraction technology, a sovereign wealth fund, an oil consumption subsidy, and membership of an international oil cartel. The calibrated model is used to simulate global risk and domestic reform scenarios the GCC economies, revealing how their distinct structural characteristics shape their responses to shocks.
focus_rationale: The paper applies a global DSGE model to the GCC countries (Gulf states), which are emerging or developing oil-dependent economies, linked to systemic advanced economies. The focus is on GCC responses to global shocks.

title: On the Role and Effectiveness of Fiscal Rules and Independent Fiscal Councils
abstract: Fiscal rules and fiscal councils are often adopted independently: many countries operate under fiscal rules without a fiscal council, while fiscal councils are frequently established only after a fiscal rule is already in place, suggesting that the two institutions may contribute differently to fiscal discipline. This paper starts with a simple theoretical framework to explain these stylized facts, accounting for the fact that governments, or even society at large, may not always be in favour of a fiscal council. The model also predicts that a sufficient strengthening of a budget balance rule, an independent fiscal council, and an increased interaction between rule strength and council strength all help reduce the expected deficit. The ensuing empirical analysis, using the updated 2025 IMF datasets on fiscal rules and fiscal councils, tests these predictions for a large country sample, including 32 advanced economies and 58 emerging market and developing economies spanning from 2000 to 2024. We find indicative evidence that, depending on the sample and the institutional design, both stronger rules and councils are associated with lower primary deficits, reduced projection biases and improved forecast accuracy. We also find some role for the interaction between the strengths of rules and councils, although the pattern varies.
focus_rationale: The paper studies a large cross-country sample of 32 advanced economies and 58 emerging market and developing economies from 2000 to 2024, so it covers both groups without a particular focus on either.

title: Options for Tax System Reform in Asia and the Pacific
abstract: Asian and Pacific economies face mounting fiscal pressures from high and rising debt and interest rates and significant spending needs in light of successive shocks. In the coming years, these fiscal strains will likely be exacerbated by the fiscal implications of structural trends in demography, technology, geoeconomic fragmentation, and climate transitions. To address these mounting fiscal challenges, domestic revenue mobilization will be imperative. Based on a comparative analysis with global peers, this paper provides an integrated assessment of the opportunities for enhanced revenue mobilization across the region, drawing on newly compiled data and indicators for cross-country revenue, tax design and tax administration. It documents comparatively low tax-to-GDP ratios and sizable tax potential, alongside marked differences in policy design and administrative capacity across income groups. The paper identifies five areas for reform for Asian and Pacific countries: strengthening value-added taxation; rationalizing corporate income tax incentives; expanding recurrent property taxation; accelerating digitalization in tax administration; and building public trust in tax administration. The appropriate sequencing differs across countries, but durable domestic revenue mobilization requires policy and administration to be treated as an integrated system, embedded in medium-term revenue strategies, and adapted to structural transitions and institutional capacity.
focus_rationale: The paper covers tax reform across many Asian and Pacific economies, spanning both advanced and emerging members, so it is regional rather than focused on one market group. It is a cross-country comparative study of fiscal revenue design.

title: The Macroeconomic Impact of AI Access Disruptions
abstract: This paper estimates the macroeconomic impact from shutting off a country’s access to frontier AI services, once that country has grown to rely on them as an input to its economy. Applied through the production network framework of Baqaee and Farhi (2019) and calibrated to a representative small open economy, the headline GDP loss from “AI sanctions” is 0.20 percent. The range of possible outcomes can vary significantly, however, depending on the future convergence path of competitor models and on the substitutability of AI across sectors. In the most severe scenario, the economic impact reaches 0.41 percent of GDP.
focus_rationale: The paper uses a generic representative small open economy calibrated in a production network framework rather than studying a specific country or group of economies.

title: Deconstructing the Stablecoin Sandwich
abstract: Stablecoins are presented as a low-cost alternative to traditional cross-border payment channels, but evidence to support this claim remains limited. We develop a cost accounting framework that traces the full “stablecoin sandwich'”: fiat in, stablecoin transfer, fiat out. We manually collect data on costs from publicly available information across 270 directed corridors covering 18 countries, 29 exchanges, and over 4,000 complete routes. Assuming users select the cheapest options for fiat on- and off- ramps, we estimate that the average cost of a $200 transfer is around 2 percent across all corridors, below the G20 target of 3 percent and cheaper than traditional remittances on average. However, in roughly one-third of corridors where granular information on costs through traditional routes is available, the cheapest traditional provider offers a lower cost than the cheapest stablecoin route. Trading fees and fiat rail (on- and off-ramp) fees account for the majority of total costs, while the stablecoin premium—the deviation of local exchange prices of stablecoins from benchmark exchange rates—is the primary driver of cross-corridor variation, pushing costs below zero in some corridors and above 8 percent in others.
focus_rationale: The paper measures stablecoin transfer costs across 270 corridors in 18 countries, spanning both advanced and emerging economies with no particular focus on either group.

title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
abstract: Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.
focus_rationale: The paper studies school phone pouch policies across US schools, an advanced economy. It is applied education economics with no macro or financial angle.

title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
abstract: We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)
focus_rationale: The paper's empirical evidence centres on the United States, where it attributes the 2020 disinflation and 2021 inflation surge to demand, supply and supply chain shocks. Its port congestion index is built from global container ship data, but the macro outcomes studied are US.

title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
abstract: The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)
focus_rationale: The paper estimates inflation attention thresholds using US inflation and expectations data and models the inflation surge and disinflation, which are US-centred advanced economy dynamics.

title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)
focus_rationale: The paper studies the US South during and after the Reconstruction era, an advanced economy, through historical political and social outcomes. It has no market, pricing or macro angle beyond a passing economic-history link.

title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)
focus_rationale: The paper uses firm-to-firm transaction data from Pakistan to study how flood-affected firms adapt their supplier networks and locations. Pakistan is an emerging economy, so the focus is EM.

title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)
focus_rationale: The paper uses linked employer-employee data from Brazil and a Brazilian court ruling on collective agreement continuation to study union bargaining effects. It is focused on a single emerging economy.

title: Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
abstract: Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)
focus_rationale: The abstract models household spending and fiscal stimulus checks using US-style household consumption data and the AER framing points to the United States, which is an advanced economy. The paper does not explicitly name a country, so the focus is inferred as DM.

title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)
focus_rationale: The paper studies residential segregation and public service access across neighborhoods in India, an emerging economy, with comparisons to the US only as a benchmark.

title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
abstract: Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)
focus_rationale: The paper studies US federal R&D appropriations and US business-sector productivity, so it is mainly about an advanced economy.

title: Reproducible Aggregation of Sample-Split Statistics
abstract: Statistical inference is often simplified by sample splitting. This simplification comes at the cost of the introduction of randomness not native to the data. We propose a simple procedure for sequentially aggregating statistics constructed with multiple splits of the same sample. The user specifies a bound and a nominal error rate. If the procedure is implemented twice on the same data, the nominal error rate approximates the chance that the results differ by more than the bound. We illustrate the application of the procedure to several widely applied econometric methods. (JEL C20, C30, C52)
focus_rationale: This is a methodological paper on sample-splitting and reproducible aggregation of statistics, with no application to a specific economy; its econometric methods are general rather than country- or market-specific.

title: The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)
focus_rationale: The paper uses high-frequency data from the European carbon market (EU ETS), whose participants are mainly advanced European economies, so the evidence is centred on DM economies such as the euro area.

title: Measuring Euro-Area Inflation Risk with Options: Market-Implied Distribution and Balance of Risks
abstract: Inflation options contain information about the entire distribution of future inflation, but extracting that information requires methodological choices regarding volatility modelling, tail behaviour and forward-distribution construction. This paper compares alternative parametric and nonparametric approaches for recovering market-implied inflation distributions and assesses how those choices affect the resulting measures of inflation risk.
focus_rationale: The paper studies euro-area inflation options to recover market-implied inflation distributions, so it is about a single advanced economy bloc. It directly concerns inflation pricing and balance of risks a strategist could use.

title: B2B Payments: How Instant Payments May Facilitate Straight-Through Processing for Businesses
authors: Routh, Aditi; Issacson, Ken; Hayashi, Fumiko; Albers, Todd; Baird, Sam
abstract: Compared with other payment methods, instant payments have unique or enhanced features, including “request for payment,” business directories, confirmation of payee, use of the international messaging standard, around-the-clock service availability, and instantaneous, irrevocable funds availability. When these features are more fully developed, instant payments may better facilitate straight-through processing for businesses than other electronic payment methods.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
focus_rationale: The paper concerns instant payment systems and business-to-business payment processing as discussed by a US Federal Reserve bank, implying a US focus. It studies payment infrastructure rather than a specific economy's market dynamics.

title: Goodfriend Memorial Lecture: Automation, Learning and Career Dynamics
abstract: Introduced in 2023, the Goodfriend Memorial Lecture series honors the legacy of Marvin Goodfriend, long-time Richmond Fed economist, research director and senior policy advisor. The lecture is delivered as part of the Richmond Fed's Collaboration of Research Economists (CORE) Week model, which brings together Richmond Fed economists and visiting economists from a range of disciplines for seminars, conferences, networking and collaboration.
focus_rationale: The abstract describes a memorial lecture series and CORE Week event format rather than a substantive study of any economy; no specific market or country is analysed.

title: What volatility reveals: Agnostic identification of exchange rate and treasury-market dynamics in inconvenient times | Lucas ter Steege, Sofia Velasco
abstract: Why did the US dollar depreciate and long-term US Treasury yields rise after the April 2025 U.S. tariff announcements even though markets clearly moved into “risk-off” mode? We address this puzzle using high-frequency asset price data and a flexible econometric approach that exploits changes in volatility to let the data themselves speak about the mechanisms at work. Our findings show that the episode cannot be understood as the effect of a single tariff shock. Rather, it reflects the interaction of safe-haven demand, confidence in U.S. institutions, Treasury-market intermediation, and changes in the convenience value of dollar-denominated safe assets. This combination helps explain why the dollar weakened in spite of an initial flight to safety. A tariff shock unlike previous tariff shocks We study the financial market impact of the US tariff announcement made on 2 April 2025. The US Administration imposed tariffs on almost all trading partners, including a 10 % baseline tariff on imports from 180 countries and an additional “reciprocal” component linked to bilateral trade imbalances. On the day of the announcement, markets behaved as we would expect in a global risk-off episode: equity prices fell, volatility spiked, and investors sought safety. However, in the days that followed, two features stood out: the US dollar depreciated against the euro, while long-term US Treasury yields rose. This pattern is at odds with both standard safe haven behavior and canonical open economy trade theory. In typical global risk episodes, higher risk premia result in a stronger dollar and lower US yields as investors rush into dollar-denominated safe assets. Furthermore, in dominant currency models of trade, tariffs imposed by a country like the United States tend to appreciate its currency via expenditure switching. Earlier US tariff episodes, such as the 2018‑2019 trade war, fit these predictions: they were associated with dollar appreciation and compressed term spreads. The 2025 episode, however, did not. We therefore question whether the April 2025 market reaction can be explained by a single “tariff shock,” or whether it reflects the interaction of multiple, distinct financial shocks. Two key shocks: safe haven and U.S. Institutional Credibility The heteroskedastic VAR model statistically identifies a set of structural shocks. We focus on the two that are most relevant for the “Liberation Day” episode. The first is a safe haven shock that captures a conventional global risk-off event. In response to such a shock, equity prices fall together with yields on long-term US Treasury yields. At the same time, the dollar appreciates against the euro as demand increases for US safe assets in response to a rise in market volatility. The second shock has a very different dynamic pattern and is crucial for understanding the post-announcement dynamics. US long-term Treasury yields rise and the exchange rate depreciates against the euro . We interpret this as a deterioration in confidence in the institutional and policy environment underpinning the international role of the United States and label it as a US Institutional Credibility shock. How these shocks explain the “Liberation Day” and why 2019 was different We use historical decompositions to quantify how much each shock contributed to the observed movements in asset prices around April 2025 and, for comparison, around the August 2019 tariff escalation. In the case of the April 2025 event, we find that the safe haven shock explains most of the fall in equity prices and the spike in volatility. The episode initially looks like a standard global risk-off event. In the subsequent days, the unusual combination of a weaker dollar and higher long-term US yields are driven primarily by the US Institutional Credibility shock. This shock becomes dominant after the initial market reaction, accounting for the persistent depreciation of the dollar and the widening of the US term spread. In the case of the August 2019 tariff escalation, by contrast, we find that this episode is largely explained by shocks with a safe haven profile and that the US Institutional Credibility shock plays a minor role. Term spreads compress and the dollar behaves in the same way as during a typical safe haven episode, in line with earlier findings on trade war episodes. This comparison shows that April 2025 was not just a “bigger 2019.” Rather, it activated an additional mechanism: a rise in Treasury risk premia that weakened the dollar and raised long-term yields, on top of the initial risk-off response. Ter Steege, L., S. Velasco (2026), What volatility reveals: Agnostic identification of exchange rate and treasury-market dynamics in inconvenient times, Bundesbank Discussion Paper, No 34/2026
focus_rationale: The paper studies US Treasury yields and the US dollar against the euro around the April 2025 tariff announcement and the August 2019 escalation, so it is about advanced economies, mainly the US and euro area.

title: El uso de la inteligencia artificial por parte de las empresas españolas: avances recientes y factores asociados a su uso
abstract: The adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies by Spanish firms increased markedly between 2024 and 2026, but remains highly uneven by firm size, sector and intensity of use. This Occasional Paper analyses recent AI adoption patterns using evidence from the Banco de España Business Activity Survey and links these data to firm balance sheet information to identify the characteristics that support AI diffusion and the barriers that continue to constrain it.
focus_rationale: The paper studies AI adoption by Spanish firms using Banco de España survey and balance sheet data, so it focuses on Spain, an advanced euro area economy.

title: ES - 2026-10-29 - Damien Klossner, Igor Mlikota and Sabrina Stadelmann: What collateral is used in the Swiss interbank repo market?
abstract: Collateral is a key component of repurchase agreement transactions. We document collateral usage in the Swiss interbank repo market using an extensive transaction-level dataset. We find that a substantial share of securities eligible for the SNB General Collateral Basket is actively used, particularly securities denominated in Swiss francs. Collateral usage is concentrated in a small number of issuers and highly rated securities denominated in Swiss francs. At the same time, it displays a broad and balanced maturity profile, and cross-currency repos account for a meaningful share of trading volume.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the Swiss interbank repo market and collateral usage in Swiss francs, which is an advanced economy. Its cross-currency repo element is tied to Swiss franc securities.

title: Building AI on credit: structures and spillovers
abstract: Capital expenditure to build artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure is growing fast, and a rising share is financed with long-term debt and through complex off-balance sheet arrangements.
focus_rationale: The abstract describes AI infrastructure financing trends in general terms without naming specific economies, so the paper appears to be cross-country or global in scope.

title: Rethinking Zombie Firms
abstract: The literature characterizes zombie firms as economically unviable companies that continue to operate. This paper proposes that the majority of zombie firms can be viable, with positive continuation value, and arise endogenously from productivity shocks. Drawing on firm-level data covering the universe of Canadian firms and seven European countries, we document five stylized facts: zombie firms are widespread, unprofitable, unproductive, micro-sized, and transitory. We rationalize these findings by building a general equilibrium model of heterogeneous firms that abstracts from the conventional distortions thought to explain zombie firms. We show that standard productivity shocks are sufficient to explain the empirical patterns, and that the volatility of these shocks can be a key determinant of viable zombie firms, generating shares up to 35%. Since this volatility can also raise aggregate productivity and household utility, the presence of zombie firms is not a sufficient condition for lower welfare. Using a model-based definition to distinguish viability, we find limited evidence—around 0.25%—of unviable zombie firms in the data. Our results challenge the prevailing view that persistently weak firms are unviable and suggest that existing zombie firm measures likely capture viable firms.
focus_rationale: The paper uses firm-level data for Canada and seven European countries, all of which are advanced economies, so it is DM. It is a cross-country study of firm dynamics rather than a focus on any single economy.

title: Coasian Stakeholder Theory
abstract: Stakeholder theory asks who is in, who is out, and who gets what.Existing work illuminates important dimensions of firm-stakeholder relationships but does not supply a common, transaction-level rule connecting these questions.We use the Coase theorem to develop such a rule.A Coasian stakeholder is an actor with shutdown power, defined as the de facto capacity, within the relevant time horizon, to prevent, materially delay, or substantially reduce the expected joint value of a focal value-creating transaction.If all such actors are identified and bargaining and enforcement are costless, value-maximizing transactions proceed, although rights and bargaining positions may affect who captures value.When transaction costs are positive, however, identification, bargaining, coalition formation, and enforcement can delay, distort, or suppress those transactions.Across six propositions, we explain how shutdown power is identified and acquired, how complementarity and bargaining conditions shape value capture, how firms reshape stakeholder sets through coalition costs and governance design, and why consolidated opposition can sometimes preserve transactions that fragmented claims would suppress.
focus_rationale: This is a theoretical paper on stakeholder theory and the Coase theorem applied to firm-stakeholder transactions, with no particular economy studied.

title: Behavioral Finance at 40
abstract: Behavioral finance seeks to improve our understanding of markets, investors, and firms by adopting a psychologically realistic description of how people think.While behavioral finance ideas have been part of human discourse for decades if not centuries, the modern research effort in the field began in the 1980s.Forty years later, behavioral finance is a vibrant area of financial economics.In this article, I explain why by reviewing some of its recent progress.I focus on three topics -beliefs about future earnings, beliefs about future returns, and prospect theory -and on their applications to understanding asset prices and investor behavior.I close by commenting on some new directions in the field -cognitive foundations, non-traditional decision processes, and artificial intelligence.
focus_rationale: The paper is a review of behavioral finance research covering asset prices and investor behavior in general, without a specific economy or region as its focus.

title: Who Can Control Our Firms? National Security and Foreign Ownership Regulation
abstract: Governments invoke national security to regulate foreign acquisitions of domestic firms.Why is ownership regulation a distinct policy margin beyond standard tools, like production subsidies and trade taxes?We show that contractual frictions make multinational firm boundaries central to geoeconomic policy.Within firms, ownership allocates residual control that affects outcomes through non-contractible decisions.Between governments, the absence of enforceable agreements makes the economic costs of conflict shape geopolitical bargaining.Foreign ownership depends on private returns to foreign control, but also determines national exposure to geopolitical conflict.It can increase foreign dependence, technology transfer, or sabotage scope.If such margins were contractible, the government could regulate them directly.When they are not, ownership regulation is the second-best tool that changes control rights and, thus, geopolitical outcomes.Consistent with our mechanism, U.S. regulation emphasizes the nationalsecurity risks of foreign control over firm decisions, has tightened with rising geopolitical tensions, and is tighter in sectors with higher exposure to defense demand and contractual frictions.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US regulation of foreign ownership of domestic firms on national security grounds, with the US as the central economy analysed.

title: Tariff Staggering
abstract: Using a panel of U.S. imports and customs duties at the HS 6-digit level, we document that in a typical quarter about 20 percent of tariffs rise, 20 percent fall, and 60 percent remain unchanged.Motivated by these facts, we develop a model of staggered tariff setting and embed it in a dynamic open-economy framework.Staggering changes the dynamics of the cross-sectional mean tariff, generating hump-shaped macroeconomic responses to tariff shocks.Staggering also overturns the Razin-Svensson trade-balance neutrality result for permanent tariff increases, because the gradual adjustment of the mean tariff creates an anticipation effect that induces agents to front-load net imports.Inherited tariff dispersion has first-order macroeconomic effects, allowing tariff harmonization to be studied with linear approximation methods.We find that eliminating tariff dispersion while holding the mean tariff unchanged has effects akin to a transitory tariff cut in an economy without staggering.
focus_rationale: The empirical panel is of U.S. imports and customs duties, and the model is a dynamic open-economy framework calibrated to the U.S. setting, so the paper is mainly about an advanced economy.

title: Ratings, Debt, and Deficits: An Exploration
abstract: We look at the effects of debt and primary fiscal balances on sovereign credit ratings through the lens of a simple model.We find that the ratings differ from the implications of the model in three important ways.They give much more weight to debt relative to forecast primary balances.They understate the effects of the difference between the interest rate and the growth rate.They give a very large role to country effects.For the same level of debt and forecast primary balances, they imply extremely different ratings across countries, and imply extremely different levels of debt needed to reach a given rating.
focus_rationale: The paper studies sovereign credit ratings across countries through a simple model of debt and primary balances, with no single economy as the focus. It is cross-country in scope.

title: When Cash Wakes Up: Inertia in Institutional Money Market Funds and the Potential Effects of AI Disruption
abstract: We study institutional cash management by constructing a novel dataset that records the specific money market funds (MMFs) held by each mutual fund in each month from 2010 to 2024.We document remarkably high inertia: more than half of mutual funds never switched their MMF choice throughout the sample period, despite non-negligible yield dispersion.To decompose the sources of this inertia, we develop a two-stage structural model that separately identifies the determinants of portfolio managers' attentiveness ("waking up") and their conditional preferences once attentive.We estimate the model using a methodology that combines BLP-style contraction mapping with maximum likelihood.We establish three main findings.First, MMFs with less attentive investor bases engage in greater liquidity transformation while offering lower yields.As a result, they earn higher profits and exhibit significantly higher survival rates, especially during periods of low interest rates.Second, we find that aggregate flows appear more yield-sensitive during low interest rate periods (the well-documented "reaching for yield" phenomenon) not because individual investors become more yield-seeking, but because a larger fraction of investors becomes attentive-a composition effect rather than a preference shift.Third, counterfactual analysis reveals a potential tension between market efficiency and financial stability if AI-driven automation reduces investor inattention.In the absence of inattention, fees fall by approximately half, yield dispersion collapses to near zero, and market concentration declines by roughly 20%, but monthly fund flows increase by about three times and the incidence of fund-months in which redemptions exceed a fund's weekly liquid assets rises by about six times, raising the risk of fire sales and MMF runs.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US institutional money market funds and the mutual funds that hold them, using data from 2010 to 2024, so it concerns an advanced economy.

title: Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand
abstract: How competitive will the market for generative AI be as it matures?Using novel transaction level credit and debit card data covering 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions, we study the adoption of paid services and the demand-side foundations of competition in this market.As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers.Nearly all of these paid users subscribe to basic plans that cost $30 or less per month.Three patterns suggest limited differentiation and low switching costs.First, although multihoming is common, it has declined as providers' capabilities have expanded.Second, annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, lower than those for many other subscription products.Third, switching rises around major model releases.Motivated by these findings, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply that reveals strong competitive pressure.Consumers are highly price sensitive, have much weaker preferences for particular providers than for AI overall, and view AI services as increasingly close substitutes.Our results suggest that, absent a substantial increase in AI model quality differentiation, growing substitutability among services will constrain providers' pricing power and allow consumers to capture a large share of the surplus generated by these services.
focus_rationale: The paper uses US consumer card transaction data to study adoption and competition in generative AI services, so it is focused on the United States, an advanced economy.

title: The Great Game: A Model of Geoeconomic Competition
abstract: We build a model of two hegemons that have valuable trading relationships with each other and at the same time compete in exerting geoeconomic power over countries in the rest of the world.When the hegemons trade with each other, their optimal policy is shaped both by classic economic considerations -the profitability of that specific trade -and by geoeconomic competition -how the trade affects the power of each hegemon vis-a-vis the rest of the world.We show that containment, a policy mix in which a hegemon limits sales of its inputs to the rival hegemon and uses its power to demand that the rest of the world shift away from sourcing from the rival, arises when the two hegemons offer relatively substitutable exports, are less interdependent with each other, and have more direct geopolitical rivalry.Countries in the rest of the world benefit, all else equal, from hegemons containing each other since they partially squander their power with offsetting demands.However, containment policy can also worsen the efficiency of global production, leaving the rest of the world worse off.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical model of two hegemons competing over the rest of the world, with no particular focus on either advanced or emerging economies.

title: A Network Approach to Geopolitics
abstract: We develop a tractable framework for analyzing geopolitics as a network of coordination and strategic influence.Countries choose geopolitical actions that trade off domestic interests against incentives to align with connected countries.They can exert costly bilateral influence to affect one another's actions.We characterize equilibrium actions and bilateral influence in closed form.Cross-country differences in domestic interests decompose into latent geopolitical cleavages, each of which the network transmits into geopolitical actions independently of the others.The crosscountry covariance matrices of domestic interests and of geopolitical actions identify the cleavages and their importance, from which we recover the network.We implement the framework using data on United Nations voting and democratic orientation.The inferred network is well approximated by a few dimensions, aligns with external measures of geopolitical ties, and recovers well-known historical cleavages.We undertake counterfactuals for domestic interests and network connections and quantify three notions of geopolitical power
focus_rationale: The paper develops a general theoretical and methodological framework for geopolitics as a network, applied to UN voting and democratic orientation across many countries with no particular focus on either advanced or emerging economies.

title: Training Your Replacement: Worker Incentives and the Pace of Automation
abstract: Firms ask workers to train AI systems that will replace them.We model this with a worker who can shirk, cooperate with training, or obstruct training while maintaining productivity.Because training ends the job but only cooperation completes training, dismissal becomes a weaker penalty for shirking.The firm must raise the worker's rent, and the worker gains from their replacement.AI can create jobs paying more than they produce and eliminate jobs it never automates.Firms paying only wages may slow training.A credible completion bonus equal to the worker's rent without AI removes both the gain and the slowdown.
focus_rationale: This is a theoretical contract-design model of worker incentives and AI automation with no specific economy studied, so it is classed as Transversal.

title: Generative AI, Managerial Expectations, and Economic Activity
abstract: Using generative AI, we extract managers' economic expectations from over 120,000 corporate conference call transcripts.The resulting AI Economy Score predicts GDP growth, production, employment, and wages five or more quarters ahead, beyond survey forecasts and other existing measures.Industry-and firm-level scores capture sector-and firm-specific activity, and a composite of firm, industry, and macroeconomic expectations further improves forecasting power and horizon.Predictability concentrates among historically more accurate, less biased managers, consistent with an information rather than a noise channel.Managerial expectations thus offer incremental insights into economic activity, with implications for macro-and microeconomic decision-making.
focus_rationale: The paper uses US corporate conference call transcripts to forecast US GDP, production, employment and wages, so it is mainly about the US economy, which is an advanced economy.

title: fevc: Leave-Out Bias-Corrected Variance Decompositions in Stata
abstract: Variance decompositions from worker and firm fixed-effect regressions measure heterogeneity and sorting in linked data, but estimation noise can substantially bias their components.This article introduces fevc, a Stata command implementing the leave-out bias correction of Kline, Saggio, and Sølvsten (2020).It reports corrected variances of worker and firm effects, their covariance, and the variance of their sum.Researchers choose the deletion unit, treatment of controls, and weights defining the target population.The command also reports standard errors for projections of fixed effects on observed characteristics.A source-only Mata implementation runs wherever Stata runs, while a parallel Rust plugin handles large datasets.Random-projection calculations report Monte Carlo standard errors measuring numerical precision.In a public extract of Italian social-security records, the correction halves the estimated variance of firm effects and reverses the worker-firm covariance's sign.In synthetic benchmarks with 6.4 million observations and 28 threads, the Rust backend is 1.3 to 3.5 times as fast as the KSS Matlab package.Under match deletion, measured peak memory is about 30 percent of the Matlab package's.
focus_rationale: This is a Stata software tool for leave-out bias-corrected variance decompositions in worker and firm fixed-effects regressions, a methodological contribution with no particular economy focus. Its empirical illustration uses Italian social-security records, but the tool itself is general.

title: An LLM Workflow for Functional Form Sensitivity Analysis
abstract: We introduce an LLM workflow for functional form sensitivity analysis.A researcher estimates the value of an object of interest by maximizing the fit of a working model to some data.The working model assumes an arbitrary form for some function.We define sensitivity by how much it is possible to change the estimate of the object of interest, without compromising fit, by selecting a different functional form.The workflow first looks for an analytic solution.If it fails to find one, it approximates the solution via numerical methods that respect the fit constraint at each step of a solver path.The workflow yields a verifiable lower bound on the in-sample sensitivity of the researcher's estimate, and is fast in many practical situations.We illustrate with an application to the welfare cost of adverse selection in health insurance.
focus_rationale: The paper is a methodological contribution on LLM-driven functional form sensitivity analysis with no specific economies studied; its illustrative application is to health insurance adverse selection.

title: The Value of (Sub) Specialization: Evidence from Oncology
abstract: We estimate the returns to specialization in medical oncology, in which subspecialists focus on specific cancer types.Using 2.2 million Medicare chemotherapy episodes from 2008-2020, we instrument for subspecialist access with differential distance to cancer-type-specific subspecialists versus general oncologists.Access to a relevant subspecialist reduces three-year mortality by 4.5 percentage points (10 percent), without increasing Medicare spending or measured provider fragmentation.Subspecialists also increase the use of newer therapies and diagnosis-specific clinical trials.These findings show that specialization raises productivity when expertise is closely matched to the task.
focus_rationale: The paper uses Medicare chemotherapy data, so it studies the United States, an advanced economy. It is a health-economics study with no macro or financial angle.

title: Selective Admissions in Nursing Homes: Evidence from a Randomized Audit Study
abstract: It has been widely documented that patients in the US who are associated with disadvantaged demographics receive care at lower quality nursing homes.To understand the role that selective admissions may play in contributing to this pattern, we conducted a nationwide audit study of the impact of patient race, payer, and medical condition on responses to about 5,500 availability inquiries sent to about 3,000 nursing homes.We find 10-15% lower availability for Medicaid patients compared to private-pay patients and for patients with Alzheimer's disease compared to those without; these availability gaps generally increase with nursing home quality.We find no statistically significant evidence of differential availability by race.To quantify the implications of these selective admissions practices, we embed the audit study results in a model of constrained nursing home choice.We estimate that if, counterfactually, Medicaid patients had the same choice sets as their private-pay counterparts, they would attend higher quality nursing homes on average, but the private-Medicaid gap in quality would be reduced by only 5-10%.Our results suggest that supply-side availability differences by payer are widespread, but that they are unlikely to be the primary factor behind the observed gap in quality of nursing homes attended.
focus_rationale: The paper studies nursing home admissions across the United States, an advanced economy, so it is DM. It is a health-care services study with only a weak link to markets.

title: Global Entrepreneurial Talent Flows: Widely Funded, Selectively Successful?
abstract: Immigrant founders of US venture-backed startups exit successfully more often than native founders.Does this hold worldwide?Using career histories for 913,226 founder-firm pairs in 213 countries , we compare founders who build abroad (expats) or return home after foreign experience (returnees) with comparable local founders in the same country.Both expats and returnees raise early funding more often globally.Expats' success premium, however, concentrates in the US (18 percent) and UK (26 percent), especially among those entering the US through graduate school, work, or direct founding.Returnees rarely show such a premium.Capital follows mobile founders across borders, but success follows them selectively.
focus_rationale: The paper uses data covering 213 countries and compares founder outcomes globally, with specific attention to US and UK success premia, so it is cross-country rather than focused on either DM or EM.

title: Comparative Advantage and Economies of Scale under Uncertainty
abstract: We study how regional specialization patterns and welfare are affected by uncertainty and economies of scale in an open economy.We use a spatial equilibrium model with sectoral economies of scale, aggregate uncertainty, and irreversible mobility decisions made by heterogenous workers.We analytically characterize how the interactions between comparative advantage, both of workers and firms, economies of scale, and uncertainty shape specialization patterns and, hence, the gains from trade.We find empirical support for the model predictions by documenting the impact of aggregate changes in volatility of sectoral productivity on U.S. regional economies.We calibrate the model using detailed data on U.S. commuting zones and international trade, and extending hat-algebra methods to accommodate uncertainty.Quantitatively, we find that uncertainty shifts employment away from riskier sectors and locations, relative to a deterministic benchmark, lowering the U.S. aggregate gains from trade by around 20 percent.The interaction between uncertainty and scale economies brings down the benefits of specialization.For regions that would otherwise lose from trade, the presence of agglomeration forces and a more elastic labor supply mitigates those losses.
focus_rationale: The paper calibrates its model to US commuting zones and US international trade data, so it is mainly about an advanced economy. It is a trade and regional labour paper with only a weak link to markets.

title: The Returns to Temporary Migration: Experimental Evidence from the H-2A Program
abstract: In 2024, 315,000 H-2A temporary seasonal work visas were issued to agricultural workers in the US.The H-2A program is controversial: earnings are high, but critics argue that workers face poor working and living conditions and that families bear the costs of separation.We randomize H-2A seasonal visas for Mexican workers.During a single US season, migrants earn more than USD 16,000 and send 70% of these earnings to origin households.Living standards in Mexico rise: food security increases, the probability of living in poverty falls by 10 percentage points, and families invest in home improvements, durable assets, and debt reduction, with little investment in businesses or productive assets.Migration has spillovers onto the household: the mental health of household respondents worsens and they avoid higher-risk situations such as walking at night, and intra-household dynamics change.Migrants generally report satisfaction with H-2A jobs and contracts, all report that they would migrate again, and 85% do so the following season.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US H-2A visas issued to Mexican workers, so it concerns a US-Mexico labour migration program with household effects in Mexico. Its link to markets is weak, centred on development and labour outcomes rather than pricing or policy transmission.

title: Sex and Subsistence: Income Effects on Risky Sexual Behavior and Partner Selection
abstract: Whether to engage in sex and with whom are extremely consequential decisions for young women worldwide, and particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where HIV rates are high and adolescent pregnancies are common.Yet little is known about the extent to which these decisions are financially motivated.We combine a randomized controlled trial of monthly cash assistance to female students at the University of Zambia with detailed, high-frequency data on sexual behavior and partner characteristics.We find that this temporary increase in income significantly changes women's sexual behavior.Treated participants are 5.1 percentage points less likely to have sex during the treatment period, and the rate of condomless sex falls by 30%.Among women who were not sexually active at baseline, the likelihood of having sex falls by 43%, and partner quality conditional on sex greatly improves.Financial assistance also reduces financial precarity, increasing food security, mental health, and cognitive capacity.These results can be rationalized with a dynamic model of partner search in which women can choose to search for boyfriends or high-income partners who provide financial support and bargain over both transfers and condom use.We conclude that a substantial share of sexual activity is financially motivated in this setting, even in a population not typically regarded as vulnerable.Increasing young women's income may be a useful tool for reducing the negative externalities of risky sex and improving match quality.
focus_rationale: The paper studies female students at the University of Zambia, a sub-Saharan African emerging economy, using a cash transfer RCT on sexual behavior and partner selection.

title: Gender Gaps: International Evidence on the Role of Family Policy
abstract: We use Luxembourg Income Study and International Social Survey Programme microdata on 27 countries over the 1986-2019 period, augmented by policy and labor market information, to estimate the impact of family-friendly policies on gender gaps in employment, wages, earnings, and part-time work, as well as child penalties in employment and earnings.We find that longer duration of parental leave generally lowers gender gaps in wages, employment, earnings, and child penalties in employment and earnings, except for high levels of this entitlement, where further increases in leave raise gender gaps.We also find that the right to request a part-time work schedule raises relative female part-time employment but lowers employment and earnings gender gaps.Higher government expenditures for childcare lower employment, earnings, and part-time employment gender gaps as well as child employment and earnings penalties.These results are generally stronger for the less educated than for the highly educated, possibly reflecting higher costs of taking time off for highly educated women.Finally, expansion of family-friendly policies over this period can account for 24-33% of our sample's reduction in gender gaps in employment and earnings and 46-76% of the reduction in child penalties in these outcomes.The slower expansion of such policies in the United States than elsewhere accounts for 6-15% of the slower reduction in US gender employment and earnings gaps and 20% of the slower fall in the US child employment penalty.
focus_rationale: The paper pools microdata from 27 countries, covering both advanced and emerging economies, so it has no single market focus. It is a cross-country study of family policy and gender gaps.

title: Optimal Taxation of Indistinguishable Activities
abstract: Optimal tax policy frequently prescribes different tax treatments for activities that are difficult in practice for tax administrators to distinguish, such as expenditures undertaken for business versus personal purposes.We study the optimal design of income tax deductions for such expenditures under the assumption that a common deduction rate must be applied to both forms of the expenditure.The Pareto optimal common deduction turns on the relative compensated spending response for each margin, weighted by the income tax wedge.We also characterize the welfare gain from distinguishing between the two expenditure forms as a harmonic mean of the compensated responses.We illustrate both results with an application to air travel expenses.
focus_rationale: This is a theoretical public-finance paper on optimal income tax deductions with no specific economy studied; the air travel application is illustrative and not tied to a particular country.

title: Regional Variations and Productivity Puzzles in Health Care
abstract: Health care utilization per capita varies widely across the United States, yet higher utilization areas have no better patient health.In the late 2000s, this pattern was widely interpreted as evidence that health care costs could be cut substantially without harming patients, which in turn shaped the 2010 Affordable Care Act.We describe how our understanding has since evolved, emphasizing three points.First, new evidence indicates quantitatively meaningful roles for both supply-side and demand-side factors in driving regional variation in health care and in health outcomes.Second, health care productivity varies substantially across providers; improving it requires better understanding of why productivity differs.Third, we know even less about the sources of area-level productivity differences.We suggest several ways in which greater engagement with the productivity literature outside of health care could yield valuable insights.
focus_rationale: The paper studies regional variation in US health care utilization and productivity, so it is mainly about an advanced economy. Its link to markets is weak.

title: Representation, Innovation, and Product Adoption
abstract: During research and development, firms must decide which types of individuals to engage in developing and testing their products.We investigate how lowering the cost of including one group shapes its representation, subsequent innovation, and product adoption.In 2000, Medicare expanded coverage of clinical trial costs for elderly trial participants, a historically underrepresented group in drug development.This policy increases representation: trial sponsors expand trial eligibility to include elderly participants and increase the share of elderly participants.We find an immediate and large increase in the number of clinical trials for diseases common among the elderly, with the largest increase in drugs not yet approved and in approved drugs tested in new diseases.We document an increase in drug utilization of newly tested drugs among elderly individuals and analyze trial results, adverse events, and drug approvals.Our findings show how financial incentives can increase representation in product development and shift the rate, direction, and adoption of innovation to potentially benefit underserved groups.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the United States Medicare clinical trial coverage policy change in 2000 and its effects on drug development and elderly drug utilization. It is a US-focused health economics study with only a weak link to markets.

title: Implications of Policy Interventions on Eliminating Gender Gaps
abstract: This paper studies policy interventions intended to eliminate gender differences in labor market outcomes, principally wages.Because gender is an individual attribute rather than a manipulable treatment, the ideal experiment of randomly assigning gender to evaluate its effects is infeasible.Policies that remove gender labels from the employment process are the closest feasible counterpart.We quantify both the intended and unintended consequences of the policies through simulated interventions of an estimated equilibrium model of statistical discrimination with dynamic choices of education and labor market participation.In the short run the policy that requires gender free applications in the market for skilled labor eliminates wage gaps but once education choices respond the effects are attenuated.A more comprehensive policy that enforces gender free compensation reverses the wage gap in skilled markets and eliminates it in unskilled labor markets, even once education adjusts.These interventions impact college rates, the college premium gap and participation rates as well.The final section studies these interventions using a difference-in-differences (DID) approach to analyze the simulated data.With education fixed, the DID method recovers the policy effects but this is not the case once education adjusts, reflecting the effects of the intervention on both treated and control groups through equilibrium adjustments in beliefs.
focus_rationale: The paper studies a structural model of statistical discrimination and gender-blind hiring and pay policies using simulated data rather than a specific economy's data, so it has no particular country focus.

title: Tax Productivity and Economic Development: A Quantitative Macroeconomic Analysis
abstract: This paper examines the role of government capacity to collect taxes in driving economic development.We first draw on a new macro-historical database to document that tax collections relative to tax administration expenditures rise sharply with GDP per capita.We then interpret this finding in a neoclassical growth model with a tax administration sector in which labor inputs are required to raise tax revenues.Countries differ in their levels of tax productivity, capturing how effectively labor is used to raise taxes, as well as their levels of productivity in creating consumption and investment goods.Governments use tax revenues to provide public capital that complements private factors in production and to make transfers.Quantitatively, our model predicts that increases in tax productivity in low-income economies can raise GDP per capita substantially more than suggested by Hulten's theorem.
focus_rationale: The paper uses a new macro-historical database and a cross-country growth model covering countries across income levels, with no particular focus on either advanced or emerging economies.

title: Losing Their Religion
abstract: Afrim Krasniqi and Juliana Rexha for very helpful insights on Albania.This paper investigates the economic consequences of the banning of religion and does not take a stand on the ethics or morality
focus_rationale: The abstract is truncated, but the acknowledgment refers to Albania, and the paper studies the economic consequences of Albania's ban on religion, a developing economy outside the euro area.

title: Insuring Landlords
abstract: This paper shows that insuring landlords against non-payment risk can improve housing access and upward geographic mobility for fragile tenants.We study Visale, a large-scale publicly funded rent guarantee insurance policy in France, free for eligible tenants and landlords.Using administrative household and claim payout data and quasi-experimental eligibility variation by exact age, we show the guarantee increased access to private-sector rental housing, especially for immigrants, newly formed households, and low-income renters.The scheme eased long-distance mobility toward expensive, high-wage neighborhoods at a moderate fiscal cost per marginal move, though potentially displacing comparable ineligible tenants through higher rents.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Visale, a publicly funded rent guarantee scheme in France, an advanced economy in the euro area.

title: College Success: Understanding the Roles of Financial Aid, Loans, Preparation, and Incentives
abstract: Over the past four decades, the earnings gap between college graduates and non-graduates has widened substantially, prompting interest in policies aimed at promoting higher education among low-income students.A key challenge for these policies is the high college dropout rate.This paper develops a dynamic model of college enrollment and completion with rich individual heterogeneity to assess how various factors influence college attendance, dropout, and graduation.We estimate the model using data from longitudinal surveys, results of quasi-experimental studies on grant aid, and large-scale randomized controlled trials.We use the model to simulate the effects of tuition subsidies, college loans, financial incentives, and increased pre-college skills on attendance and completion.We find moderate effects of most unconditional financial policies on attendance, with small effects on completion conditional on attendance.By contrast, some meritbased incentives, such as forgiving student loans upon receipt of a bachelor's degree, have substantial effects.However, this type of policy and other financial subsidies accrue even more than the others to students from relatively wealthy backgrounds.Overall, it appears infeasible to design a financial aid policy that is simultaneously effective in raising attainment and fiscally progressive.By comparison, we find that the greatest potential for increasing attainment could come from better preparing students for college.
focus_rationale: The paper models US college enrollment, dropout and completion using US longitudinal surveys and US financial aid policy evidence, so it focuses on an advanced economy with no market link.

title: The Occupational Ladder: Implications for Life-Cycle Wage Dynamics
abstract: Some occupations pay higher wages than others, even conditional on worker characteristics, implying that occupations can be ranked on a ladder.We develop a simple decomposition to study the role this occupational ladder plays in average wage growth and in the fanning out of wages over the life cycle.We present three main findings.First, the distribution of employment shifts towards higher-paying occupations as workers gain experience.This contributes modestly to average lifecycle wage growth, with greatest impact in early career.Second, this upward movement in the occupational employment distribution is not accompanied by increasing dispersion; thus, the occupational ladder does not directly contribute to the fanning out of wages.Third, early-career workers who are well-positioned on the occupational ladder tend to earn wages far below the occupational average.However, by mid-career, workers' relative wages within occupations (their positions on the job ladder) no longer depend on their occupation.This change in the covariance between individuals' positions on the job and occupational ladders is a major contributor to the fanning out of wages over workers' careers.
focus_rationale: The abstract does not name a specific country, but NBER working papers on US labour market life-cycle wage dynamics are typically US-based, so the paper is best classed as advanced-economy focused. It is applied labour economics with only a weak link to markets.

title: Strategic Monetary Policy in Open Economies
abstract: We examine optimal non-cooperative monetary policy in a two-country New Keynesian setting with complete financial markets and pricing to market for goods.In contrast to the case in which the law of one price holds for goods, currency misalignments are an important consideration even for selforiented policymakers.Financial markets are critical in the analysis.Under "full" commitment, the optimal policy considers the effects on asset values and hence wealth distribution across countries.Optimal policy under full commitment differs from the "partial" commitment case in which the policy commitment is not made until after asset markets clear.Surprisingly, the optimal targeting rule under strategic policy with full commitment is the same as under cooperative policy.In this setting, changes in state-contingent claim prices offset the wealth a self-oriented policymaker might seek through terms-of-trade manipulation, and we show that there are no gains from cooperation.Although a policy chosen under partial commitment may be desirable from a country's perspective, the resulting Nash equilibrium yields lower welfare.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical two-country New Keynesian model with no specific economies calibrated or studied; its results apply symmetrically to both countries in the setting.

title: HouseholdBench: Evaluating Large Language Models as Predictors of Household Economic Behavior
