This paper examines whether the CST influenced banks’ loan pricing and credit allocation, particularly with respect to borrowers’ greenhouse gas ( GHG ) emissions intensity. Methodology The authors use granular loan-level data from the Eurosystem’s AnaCredit database, which provides detailed information on bank loans to non-financial corporations. Borrower-level GHG intensity is estimated using sectoral emissions data and firm turnover, allowing the study to capture transition risk exposure across a broad range of firms, including small and medium-sized enterprises. The analysis employs a difference-in-differences (DiD) framework, comparing changes in the sensitivity of loan spreads to borrower carbon intensity for banks subject to the CST (treated banks) versus those not subject to it (control banks). The study also decomposes the observed effects into intensive (within-relationship repricing) and extensive (portfolio reallocation and entry/exit) margins. Theoretical Framework The paper builds on a theoretical model in which a CST acts as an information-revelation shock, shedding light on transition risks and increasing supervisory scrutiny. This shock alters banks’ perceived risk distribution, influencing their lending decisions. The model predicts that CSTs can steepen, flatten, or leave unchanged the relationship between loan spreads and borrower carbon intensity, depending on how banks adjust their pricing and portfolio composition in response to the new information. Key Findings Aggregate Effect on Loan Pricing : On average, the CST did not significantly change the sensitivity of loan spreads to borrower carbon intensity. The post- CST shift in the spread–intensity slope was small and statistically indistinguishable from zero. Portfolio Reallocation : Treated banks reallocated credit away from more carbon-intensive incumbent borrowers, reducing their share of new lending to these firms. This reallocation was particularly pronounced among the most carbon-intensive borrowers. Entry/Exit Pricing : Treated banks charged higher spreads to new borrowers with higher carbon intensity compared to incumbents, about 10 bps more for one SD increase in carbon-intensity. This is evidence of more stringent pricing of transition risks on the extensive margin. Intensive Margin : Within existing bank–borrower relationships, there was little evidence of systematic repricing based on carbon intensity. This suggests that the CST ’s impact operated primarily through portfolio composition rather than within-relationship adjustments. No significant Heterogeneity in Treatment Intensity : Among significant institutions ( SIs ), banks that participated in the more demanding bottom-up module of the CST did not exhibit stronger changes in carbon-sensitive pricing compared to those that only participated in lighter modules. This suggests that the main behavioral adjustments stemmed from CST participation itself, rather than the depth of the exercise. Asymmetric and Nonlinear Effects : Treated banks responded more strongly to decreases in borrower carbon intensity than to increases, and the CST ’s impact was more pronounced for borrowers in the upper tail of the emissions distribution. Conclusion The ECB ’s CST influenced banks’ lending behavior primarily through portfolio reallocation and differential pricing of new relationships, rather than through uniform changes in loan pricing. Treated banks reduced their exposure to carbon-intensive borrowers and applied more stringent pricing to new high-intensity relationships, signaling a shift toward climate-sensitive credit allocation. However, the CST ’s impact on within-relationship repricing was limited, highlighting the importance of relationship dynamics and informational frictions in shaping banks’ responses to climate risks. From a policy perspective, these findings suggest that CSTs can serve as effective tools for encouraging banks to integrate climate risks into their lending decisions, even in the absence of direct capital requirements. By revealing transition risks and increasing supervisory scrutiny, CSTs can drive portfolio adjustments that align with broader climate goals. Future research could explore the real-economy implications of these adjustments, such as their impact on firm-level emissions and investment, as well as the interaction between CSTs and other climate policies. De Bandt, O., D. Nefzi, J.-G. Werner (2026), Stress testing European banks’ transition risk and lending behavior, Bundesbank Discussion Paper, No 33/2026.
focus_rationale: The paper studies euro area banks and their loan pricing to non-financial corporations in response to the ECB's 2021-22 climate stress test, so it concerns advanced economies. Its focus is bank credit allocation and transition risk rather than market pricing.

title: Headwind or tailwind? How banks interpret borrowers’ AI exposure
abstract: General-purpose technologies create large opportunities but make their distribution across firms difficult to assess in real time. We use banks as interpreters of the rise of generative AI by studying lender-specific probability-of-default (PD) estimates for private firms in four large euro-area economies. As public attention to AI rises after ChatGPT, banks lower assessed default risk for borrowers in highly AI-exposed industries by about 5%. The reassessment is weaker for labor-intensive firms and stronger among lenders with pre-existing industry expertise. Yet the favorable industry-level effect is accompanied by a systematic reordering within product markets: banks reassess firms with stronger pre-ChatGPT market positions less favorably relative to their competitors, compressing the risk advantage associated with market leadership. Credit allocation moves in the same direction, with market leaders experiencing relatively lower drawn and committed credit, more relationship exits, and fewer new lenders. The reordering also predicts subsequent bad-credit events beyond banks’ consensus PDs. Internal bank assessments therefore provide a forward-looking measure of how generative AI is expected to reshape competitive risk.
focus_rationale: The paper studies bank-assessed default probabilities for private firms in four large euro-area economies, all advanced economies. Euro area members are classed as DM.

title: Competing rails for crossborder payments: banks, fintechs, and stablecoins
abstract: Cross-border payments remain slow and expensive despite significant improvements in digital financial infrastructure over the past several decades.
focus_rationale: The paper addresses cross-border payment systems globally, comparing banks, fintechs and stablecoins without a specific economy focus.

title: Inflation after the Iran war
abstract: An unexpected increase in energy costs raises inflation directly through flexibly-set prices. Whether that shock amplifies to a larger and persistent rise in inflation depends on its transmission through the economy.
focus_rationale: The abstract discusses a general energy-cost shock and its transmission to inflation without naming specific economies, so it applies across countries rather than to one group.

title: Central banks and macro financial stability in a fragmented global economy
abstract: The 25th BIS Annual Conference took place in Basel, Switzerland on 26 June 2026. The event brought together a distinguished group of central bank Governors, leading academics and former public officials to exchange views on the theme “Central banks and macro-financial stability in a fragmented global economy”.
focus_rationale: This is a conference announcement with no specific economies studied; its theme is global, covering central banks and financial stability in a fragmented world economy.

title: Determinantes de la modalidad del tipo de interés de las hipotecas y evolución de sus márgenes durante el período de endurecimiento de la política monetaria 2022-2023
abstract: Fixed-rate mortgages in Spain have shifted over the past few years from being a minority product in new mortgage lending to becoming the dominant mortgage type. This paper investigates the factors associated with this transformation and the evolution of mortgage margins, using granular data and several econometric analyses to compare borrowers, loan contracts, and banks before and during the recent period of monetary policy tightening.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the Spanish mortgage market, a euro area economy, during the 2022-2023 monetary tightening. Spain is an advanced economy and a euro area member, so the paper is DM.

title: Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States
abstract: Katie Brinkman, Christine Dobridge , Tim Dore , Simon Glossner , Elizabeth Holmquist , Nam Nguyen, Maria Perozek , and Irina Stefanescu Over the past decade, private credit has played an increasingly important role in providing funding to middle-market businesses. While there are several definitions of private credit, here we define it as privately negotiated loans to businesses that are originated by nonbank investment funds rather than by traditional financial intermediaries such as banks.
focus_rationale: The paper introduces private credit into the US Financial Accounts, so it studies the United States economy specifically. It concerns nonbank lending to middle-market businesses.

title: Ripples in the Reserve Pool: Unveiling Liquidity Signals from the Federal Funds Market
abstract: Sriya Anbil , Sebastian Infante, and Zeynep Senyuz When the Federal Reserve shifted to an ample-reserves framework, many observers started to question the relevance of the fed funds market. With reserves ample or abundant and rates anchored by administered floors, interbank borrowing declined sharply, and the market appeared to serve mainly as an arbitrage venue for non-bank institutions.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the US federal funds market and the Federal Reserve's ample-reserves framework, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: Government Bonds’ Safe-Haven Property and Inflationary Pressures
abstract: Canlin Li and Emre Yoldas Earlier this year, escalation of the conflict in the Middle East resulted in sharp declines in major stock indexes as energy prices rose and the global economic outlook deteriorated, but prices of long-term government bonds in major advanced economies also declined (Figure 1). This prompted some commentators to question the premise that government bonds in these major advanced economies will rally in times of increased risk aversion and serve as a safe haven for investors (see for example, Kim, 2026).
focus_rationale: The note examines long-term government bonds in major advanced economies, which the abstract describes as the US and other advanced markets, responding to a Middle East conflict and energy price shock.

title: Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets
abstract: We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets. Using unique transaction-level data on the universe of centrally cleared NDFs for ten emerging-market currencies over 2013–2025, we show that offshore NDF order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates and widens the offshore–onshore forward spread.
focus_rationale: The paper studies ten emerging-market currencies using offshore NDF and onshore spot data, so it is about EM exchange rate dynamics.

title: Land concentration and large renewable energy projects
abstract: This paper examines how land ownership concentration shapes the deployment of largescale renewable energy projects across six European countries (Spain, Germany, France, Italy, Belgium and the Netherlands). Using a 5×5 km grid-cell framework with cadastral parcel data, we show that cells with a higher share of area in large parcels (≥ 10 ha) are substantially more likely to host mega photovoltaic (PV) plants (≥ 50 ha), with a standardized semi-elasticity of 68% in the pooled sample, consistent across all six countries. Land concentration also drives aggregate solar deployment: a one-standard-deviation increase raises expected PV hectares within a grid cell by 62%, an effect driven almost entirely by the mega-plant margin. By contrast, the effect on wind parks is weaker and heterogeneous, consistent with wind requiring less contiguous land assembly than solar. A specificity test and decomposition analysis corroborate that the assembly mechanism operates specifically at the mega-plant margin, and a horse race between cadastral concentration and farm operational size establishes that ownership, not farming scale, is the operative mechanism. A finer 500 m grid within-municipality analysis corroborates the effect of land concentration on mega PV plants and further reveals that it is attenuated in irrigated areas, where higher agricultural rents raise landowner reservation values. We rationalize these patterns with a conceptual framework in which solar assembly requires unanimous consent from a set of landowners whose number falls with parcel size, while wind requires only a subset. Our findings reveal that land ownership structure is a decisive factor in the energy transition: fragmentation impedes large-scale deployment, while concentration enables it but channels its benefits toward a few large landowners, potentially deepening rural grievances and local opposition.
focus_rationale: The paper studies six advanced European economies: Spain, Germany, France, Italy, Belgium and the Netherlands. All are DM, including the euro area periphery.

title: Contract design, higher yields make basis trade alternatives attractive
authors: De Vere, Hugo; McCormick, Matthew; Ramaswamy, Srini
abstract: Recent plateauing in activity involving the basis trade, in which investors buy Treasuries and sell their futures, has generated policymaker attention and questions about factors driving the shift. Among questions is the extent to which a deleveraging of Treasury holdings may be affecting demand for short-term funding.
focus_rationale: The paper concerns the US Treasury basis trade and Treasury futures markets, so it is focused on the US, an advanced economy.

title: A Brief History of Deposit Tokens and Tokenized Deposits
abstract: The tokenization of commercial bank deposits has been in development globally since the late 2010s, evolving from theory and experimentation to the more recent implementation of both deposit tokens and tokenized deposits. Tokenizing commercial bank deposits has implications for other blockchain-based payment instruments, such as stablecoins, as well as for legacy payments systems, presenting banks with new opportunities and challenges.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
focus_rationale: The paper surveys the global development of deposit tokens and tokenized deposits without focusing on a specific economy or region.

title: The Treasury General Account and the Fed’s Balance Sheet
abstract: Changes in the Treasury’s cash management practices after the COVID pandemic in-creased the Fed’s balance sheet by as much as 2 percentage points of nominal GDP, including the larger buffer required to maintain ample reserve levels. A parsimonious time-series model shows that, once we account for the impact of the Treasury’s extraor-dinary measures during debt-ceiling episodes, the observed changes in the Treasury General Account since COVID are mostly driven by higher target balances. An effec-tive sterilization program by the Fed would require timely and accurate information at high frequencies.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the US Treasury General Account and the Federal Reserve's balance sheet, so it is about a single advanced economy, the United States.

title: Offshoring and Voting Patterns in the US
abstract: This paper studies the impact of offshoring by US firms on voting patterns for incumbents in the US.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the effect of US firms' offshoring on US voting patterns, so it is about an advanced economy, the United States.

title: The Distributional Consequences of Commodity Booms
abstract: Positive commodity price shocks reduce labor income inequality in commodity-exporting economies by compressing the skill premium, as unskilled-labor-intensive sectors such as construction expand faster than skill-intensive services. A multisector small-open-economy model shows how saving or spending commodity windfalls can reinforce or moderate this decline in inequality.
focus_rationale: The abstract describes a multisector small-open-economy model of commodity-exporting economies without naming a specific country, so it is a generic cross-country theoretical study.

title: Beyond "Looking Through": Monetary Policy Responses and Communication Under Supply-Driven Inflation
abstract: Using a controlled macroeconomic experiment, we compare monetary policy rules that differ in how much they look through inflation: a Lean-Against policy with strong response to inflation and a Look-Through policy with less strong response. We combine each rule with communication protocols that vary the information the central bank releases about its policy response.
focus_rationale: The paper is a controlled macroeconomic experiment on monetary policy rules and communication under supply-driven inflation, framed around Bank of Canada policy, so it concerns an advanced economy.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Financial Tail Risks
abstract: This paper examines how market-perceived AI exposure is associated with extreme financial-sector gains and losses across five markets, using Expected Shortfall and skewness decompositions to distinguish AI-sector, macroeconomic, systemic and financial scenarios.
focus_rationale: The paper studies financial-sector tail risks across five markets, which are likely advanced economies given the Bank of Canada source, but the abstract does not name the countries explicitly. Classified as DM on the source and the market-based, financial-stability framing.

title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
abstract: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
focus_rationale: The paper studies US public firms' revenue per worker, profit margins and productivity using 10-K filings, so it is about a single advanced economy.

title: When less is more: behavioral effects of CBDC holding limits
abstract: Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies (CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance, they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect. This effect is material only when the limit is high enough. Enabling reverse waterfall —automatic conversion into this limited means of payment— increases adoption while reducing holdings. These results suggest that combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms can support CBDC use while containing holdings, thereby helping to mitigate potential financial stability risks.
focus_rationale: The experiment recruits participants from four euro-area countries, all advanced economies, so the paper is about DM retail CBDC design in the euro area.

title: Stop believing in haircuts - at least the way you think about them
abstract: We study how frictions impact haircut setting in repo markets. Using transaction-level supervisory data and exploiting the 2021 introduction of the binding leverage ratio requirement, we show that three frictions jointly shape haircuts in the bilateral dealer-to-client segment: dealer balance sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. In collateral-driven repos, binding leverage constraints and broader client outside options both raise haircuts, while higher convenience yields push them down. In funding-driven trades, the leverage constraint has no effect, higher convenience yields raise haircuts through the rehypothecation channel, and broader client outside options lower them. We rationalise these patterns in a bilateral bargaining model with periodic haircut renegotiation. Consistent with the model, constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility and weaker pass-through of ECB policy rate changes in the collateral-driven segment. Post-crisis bank regulation thus carries potential unintended consequences for repo market functioning and the transmission of monetary policy.
focus_rationale: The abstract uses transaction-level supervisory data on the bilateral dealer-to-client repo segment and does not name specific economies. Its focus is euro-area-style repo markets and ECB policy pass-through, but the paper's economies are not explicitly stated, so it is classed as Transversal.

title: Chokepoint disruptions and their macroeconomic consequences
abstract: Rising geopolitical tensions, including trade restrictions and conflicts, are increasingly disrupting global supply chains, posing significant risks at critical chokepoints. Strong substitution effects and the use of inventories have helped to mitigate adverse output effects of chokepoint disruptions, but they often come at the cost of higher input prices. An effective policy response to chokepoint disruptions requires a tailored approach that takes account of the cause, centrality and the private sector’s ability to substitute and draw on buffers.
focus_rationale: The paper studies supply-chain chokepoint disruptions in general terms, with no particular economy as its focus, so it is cross-country and global in scope.

title: Firm Pay and Consumption Inequality
abstract: An extensive body of research has documented that firms play an important role in wage inequality. However, much less is known about how firm pay differentials translateinto household spending, and under what conditions those spending differences map into welfare differences. In this paper, we combine newly collected expenditure data with employer-employee records from Norway to examine how firm pay inequality is transmitted to household spending. We show that when workers move up the firm pay ladder, the resulting increase in spending is roughly half of the increase in disposable income: the implied marginal propensity to consume (MPC out of income) is approximately 0.5. These spending responses are highly persistent. The response is concentrated in discretionary and housing-related spending: hotel stays display the largest relative response, while housing-related expenditures account for the largest share of the aggregate MPC. Next, we decompose wages and spending into worker- and firm-level components, and find that firms account for roughly half the variance in consumption inequality relative to wages. Finally, a search model with consumption-savings decisions reproduces these results and shows that firm-level consumption differences closely track firms’ contribution to welfare inequality. Our findings thus indicate that firms play an important role not only in wage inequality but also in welfare inequality.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Norwegian households and employer-employee records, a single advanced economy. It links firm pay differentials to household spending and MPCs, which is an indirect macro link to consumption and housing.

title: Price Rigidities in the Market for New Homes
abstract: We study pricing and liquidity in the market for new housing using rich project-level and transaction-level data from Norway. We provide evidence that points to prices of new homes adjusting substantially more sluggishly than prices in the existing-home market. A central empirical fact is that the relative price growth of new versus existing homes comoves positively with inventory-to-sales ratios in the new-housing market. In the cross-section, we further show that higher initial prices are associated with longer selling durations, delayed project starts, and higher cancellation probabilities. We interpret these findings through a simple theoretical framework with imperfect substitutability between new and existing housing and rigid prices for new homes. The model is consistent with the observed joint dynamics of relative prices, sales, and inventories under housing-demand shocks, while alternative flexible-price mechanisms or other shocks cannot generate these comovements. Overall our findings suggest that price rigidities among developers amplify housing-demand shocks and may contribute to persistent fluctuations in residential investment and housing supply.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the new-housing market in Norway, an advanced economy, using project-level and transaction-level data.

title: Behavioral Expectations in Nonlinear DSGE Models
abstract: Cognitive discounting has become a workhorse device for bounded rationality in monetary economics. It is specified on perceived states or on selected expected terms and used mostly in linearized models, while the questions it is asked to answer — the effective lower bound, large shocks, risk, regime change — are intrinsically nonlinear. This paper introduces a variable-specific behavioral-expectations operator, defined directly on the nonlinear equilibrium conditions of DSGE models, including nonstationary and regime-switching ones. Before the rational expectation is taken, the operator contracts selected forward-looking variables toward reference points, in stated coordinates. The reference points may move over time or depend on the regime. At first order the operator reproduces Gabaix’s (2020) one-step discounting of expectations, except that each selected variable is discounted in every equation in which it appears. At second order and above it discounts risk : each variable’s k-th conditional cumulant of one-step deviations from its reference point, in the chosen coordinates (logs or levels), is scaled by the k-th power of its attention. This can turn divergent conditional expectations into convergent ones, a candidate structural complement to pruning. We illustrate the methodology by estimating a nonstationary nonlinear New Keynesian model with an occasionally binding lower bound on pre-2020 US data. With attention estimated variable by variable, the data decisively prefer cognitive discounting to rational expectations, by about 14 log points of marginal likelihood. Posterior mean attention is uneven across variables. Which restrictions the data accept depends on the model and the observables.
focus_rationale: The paper estimates a nonlinear New Keynesian model on pre-2020 US data, so the economy studied is the United States, an advanced economy. The methodology is general, but the application is US monetary policy at the effective lower bound.

title: Inflation and Price Dispersion: New Cross-Sectoral and International Evidence
abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between price dispersion and inflation, shedding light on one major source of the cost of high inflation. By analyzing novel product-level web-scraped data from over 60,000 restaurants and supermarkets across 18 countries facing high and low inflation periods, I uncover new evidence of a significant positive correlation between inflation and price dispersion. My findings reveal that average annualized inflation, ranging between 0 and 20 percentage points across countries within a condensed time frame, is significantly associated with higher price dispersion in both the restaurant and the supermarket sectors. The estimates indicate that the marginal effect of suboptimal inflation on product-level distortions is positive, economically significant in all inflation environments and heterogeneous across sectors. Cross-sectionally, I find that as annualized inflation rises from 0% to 10% inefficient price dispersion is about 46% higher for supermarkets and 73% higher for restaurants. Lastly, the relationship between inflation and price dispersion does not flatten much at higher inflation, so that the marginal cost of additional inflation does not vanish as inflation rises – a pattern standard menu-cost models do not generate. This indicates a sustained impact of inflation on price dispersion, implying that accommodating higher inflation levels incurs substantial welfare costs.
focus_rationale: The paper uses web-scraped product prices from restaurants and supermarkets across 18 countries with both high and low inflation, so it covers both advanced and emerging economies without a particular focus on either. The specific countries are not named in the abstract.

title: The Impacts of Unauthorized Immigration on U.S. Labor and Housing Markets: New Evidence from Administrative Microdata
abstract: From early 2021 through early 2024, the U.S. experienced an unprecedented boom in unauthorized immigration, with substantial heterogeneity across local economies. Using administrative microdata, we construct new measures of national and local unauthorized immigration flows and exploit exogenous variation using multiple empirical designs. Unauthorized immigrant worker flows increased local employment approximately one-for-one, with mixed evidence of wage depression. They also raised house prices and rents without expanding housing supply. Finally, these flows reduced labor income per capita and government transfers. These findings help inform debates surrounding how unauthorized immigration impacts labor and housing markets and public finances in the U.S.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
focus_rationale: The paper studies the United States, an advanced economy, using local U.S. labour and housing market data.

title: Reserve-based lenders must adapt risk framework as energy producers package best collateral in asset-backed securities
authors: Byun, Sung Je; Monteith, Matthew T.
abstract: Banks need to develop an understanding of how this relatively new financing structure affects their competitive positioning and portfolio risk management.
focus_rationale: The paper concerns US energy producers and reserve-based lending by US banks, so it is centred on the United States, an advanced economy.

title: What Big Macs tell us about the disconnect between prices and exchange rates
authors: Davis, J. Scott; Kim, Ben; Zlate, Andrei
abstract: The Economist's Big Mac Index is a measure of the real exchange rate that instead of measuring the price of a basket of goods and services, measures the price of one good, the McDonald's Big Mac. Recent empirical work finds that financial factors, and not monetary ones, underlay a very high correlation between nominal exchange rates and the Big Mac-based real exchange rate.
focus_rationale: The paper uses the Big Mac Index across many countries to examine the link between nominal exchange rates and real exchange rates, with no specific regional focus.

title: Financially Distressed Consumers May Have Turned to High-Cost Credit to Cope with Inflation
abstract: Many U.S. consumers, especially those who are financially distressed, have used various strategies to cope with rising prices last year. Notably, financially distressed consumers were substantially more likely to have taken on additional debt to manage the financial strain of inflation; furthermore, they often borrowed at higher costs. Higher inflation rates and cuts in federal financial aid this year may compel even more financially distressed consumers to rely on high-cost credit.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
focus_rationale: The paper studies US consumers coping with inflation and borrowing costs, so it is about a single advanced economy.

title: Banking Analytics: Largest Banks' Trading Assets Surge in Recent Quarters
abstract: Trading assets at U.S. global systemically important banks reached $3.7 trillion in Q2 of 2026, up from $2.5 trillion at the end of 2024. They now account for about 20% of assets at U.S. GSIBs.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
focus_rationale: The paper studies trading assets at U.S. global systemically important banks, a DM economy. It is a short banking data note with a clear link to market-making, funding and financial stability.

title: Post-Hurricane Helene Housing: Where Are We Now?
abstract: In September 2024, Western North Carolina (WNC) communities sustained extensive damage from Hurricane Helene. A previous Regional Matters post highlighted that the storm’s impact was set against a backdrop of preexisting housing market tightness. Now, more than two years later, recent data provide a look at how housing market dynamics have evolved in WNC, particularly in areas that sustained the most damage.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the housing market in Western North Carolina, a region of the US, which is an advanced economy.

title: Tracking Property Investor Patterns in Seven Urban Counties in the Fourth District
abstract: This article examines trends among property investors across seven urban counties in the Fourth Federal Reserve District, including the share of single-family homes (SFHs) owned by smaller and larger investors and the market concentration of the largest SFH investors.
focus_rationale: The paper studies single-family home investors in seven urban counties of the Fourth Federal Reserve District, which is in the United States, an advanced economy.

title: Central bank independence: the foundations and limits of credible monetary policy
authors: Charles de Beauffort, Sarah El Joueidi
abstract: Recent attempts to exert political pressure on central banks have brought the issue of central bank independence back to the centre of the policy debate. Why is such independence essential for credible monetary policy? What are its limits and under what conditions can it remain effective amid the expanding scope of central bank action and high levels of public debt?
focus_rationale: The abstract is a general discussion of central bank independence and credible monetary policy without naming a specific economy, so it covers no particular country or region.

title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
abstract: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
focus_rationale: The paper studies the United States, an advanced economy, examining how the AI investment boom has affected the US current account and trade balance.

title: The Rise of Semiliquid Funds for Retail Investors
abstract: Logan George and Chaehee Shin Investment funds differ in how investors can access their capital. The redemption rules governing how and when investors can withdraw have evolved endogenously in response to shifting investor demand and regulatory constraints. While the immediate liquidity of open-end mutual funds and exchange-traded funds has long dominated the retail market, the landscape has been evolving over time.
focus_rationale: The note examines the US fund industry and retail investor access to semiliquid funds, which is a US-focused study of fund structures. It is indirectly relevant to markets via fund liquidity and redemption dynamics.

title: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
abstract: Isabel Cairó , Shigeru Fujita, and Camilo Morales-Jimenez The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US household labor supply and fiscal transfers during the COVID-19 pandemic, using CPS/ASEC data and a model calibrated to the US economy.

title: What analysts hear and why it matters for monetary policy
abstract: We introduce a novel measure of how European Central Bank (ECB) monetary policy is interpreted by analysts at major investment banks. We construct a “policy interpretation shock” based on the language used in analysts’ reports covering monetary policy decisions by the ECB’s Governing Council (GovC). The main identifying assumption is that changes in the way analysts report on policy communication by the GovC—that is, the change in the policy tone from the preview report to the recap report—reflect unexpected information revealed by the policy event. Using GPT-based sentiment extraction, we show that the tone in these reports closely tracks that of the GovC, often even anticipating shifts in tone. Changes in the policy tone before and after meetings capture how market intermediaries interpret and adjust their assessment of policy decisions. These interpretation shocks are followed by contractionary macroeconomic responses and systematic movements in financial-market prices. These findings underscore the important role of communication in shaping expectations and influencing economic outcomes.
focus_rationale: The paper studies how analysts interpret ECB monetary policy decisions and the resulting macro and financial-market responses, all in the euro area, which is an advanced economy bloc.

title: The heterogeneous bank lending channel of monetary policy
abstract: How does heterogeneity in banks’ interest-rate risk exposure shape monetary policy transmission? We develop a quantitative macroeconomic model of heterogeneous banks to answer this question. We establish an irrelevance result: differences in interest-rate risk exposure between fixed- and variable-rate banking systems matter for transmission only when bank solvency concerns become relevant. Calibrating the model to the euro area, we show that idiosyncratic default risk pushes a substantial share of banks toward the solvency threshold, making heterogeneity quantitatively important. When policy rates rise, fixed-rate banks suffer net interest margin compression—funding costs increase while legacy loan income stays unchanged—eroding capital and triggering sharper deleveraging. The lending elasticity to monetary policy is one-third larger in fixed-rate economies. The effects extend to financial stability: tightening raises bank failure rates in fixed-rate systems while lowering them in variable-rate systems. The results provide a rationale for macroprudential and monetary policy coordination and for monetary policy gradualism.
focus_rationale: The paper calibrates a quantitative model to the euro area, a advanced economy, and studies how monetary policy transmits through bank interest-rate risk exposure there.

title: Money and the architecture of trust
abstract: Money is one of the most consequential social institutions humanity has built. Starting from the most elementary monetary act, a payment, this paper provides an account of how money works, grounded in the tradition of credit theories of money.
focus_rationale: The paper is a conceptual account of how money works, grounded in credit theories of money, with no particular country or economy as its focus.

title: How is Labor Demand Changing as AI Improves? New Global Evidence
abstract: The rapid advance of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has sparked intense debate about its effects on labor markets. We draw on over 700 million online job postings to present new evidence covering 110 economies. Demand has declined by nearly 10 percent in more AI-exposed occupations but, surprisingly, this impact has stabilized even as AI has become more capable. To understand this pattern, we develop a novel measure of AI adoption based on references to emerging AI skills in job postings. Demand for these skills has grown rapidly, particularly in more exposed occupations. Indeed, firms with stronger demand for AI skills exhibit faster growth in job postings, even in more exposed occupations. AI appears to be reshaping labor demand by both compressing hiring in more exposed occupations and generating new opportunities for workers with AI skills.
focus_rationale: The paper uses job postings from 110 economies spanning advanced and emerging markets, so it is cross-country rather than focused on either group.

title: Inverted Gravity
abstract: We invert structural gravity to recover trade cost changes delivering targeted outcomes.For attainable welfare targets, one instrument per target yields a unique solution.At unchanged producer prices and to first order, each instrument must change by the welfare target divided by its own expenditure share; the required domestic change is about the size of the target, while the import change is several times larger.Inverting observed trade flows gives a separate trade cost change for each of the two directions in which a pair of countries trades.Applications to NAFTA and world trade illustrate the benefits of our approach.
focus_rationale: The paper develops an inversion method for structural gravity models of trade costs and welfare, applied to NAFTA and world trade, so it is methodological and cross-country rather than focused on one market group.

title: When Cash Flows Turn Negative: Liquidity-Driven Selling by Pension Funds
abstract: Pension funds are long-horizon investors with predictable liability structures.As such, they are often perceived as investors who can provide liquidity and stabilize markets.However, pension funds increasingly face negative operating cash flows as benefit payments exceed contributions.Using aggregate data on U.S. public pension funds combined with granular holdings obtained through public records requests, we document three findings that challenge the conventional view of pension funds as stabilizing investors.First, pension funds with more negative cash flows do not adjust their target asset allocations and maintain low allocations to safe and liquid assets.Second, because of these limited safe asset buffers, pension funds meet cash flow shocks primarily by selling equities, absorbing $0.67 per dollar of shock through equity sales.At the security level, pension funds sell across equities rather than following a safe and liquid-assets-first approach.Third, pension funds sell equities even when equity returns are negative, indicating that these trades reflect liquidity needs rather than portfolio rebalancing.Together, these findings show that pension funds have become regular sellers in equity markets rather than contrarian, stabilizing investors.
focus_rationale: The paper studies U.S. public pension funds and their equity selling behaviour, so the economy studied is the United States, an advanced economy.

title: Do Judges Move Markets? Ideological Shifts in the Supreme Court and Macroeconomic Expectations
abstract: This paper studies how judicial ideology shapes financial markets' expectations about the macroeconomy.We use unexpected deaths of U.S. Supreme Court Justices as quasi-experimental shifts in the Court's ideological balance.High-frequency asset price responses reveal how markets perceive the macroeconomic consequences of these ideological shifts.We find that a more conservative Court is associated with lower inflation expectations, lower real activity expectations, and lower bond yields.A shift towards a more liberal Court induces the opposite responses.The finding that inflation and activity expectations respond with the same sign suggests that markets revise their expectations about aggregate demand, rather than aggregate supply.Moreover, contrasting the yield responses with estimates from studies of fiscal policy news indicates that a more conservative (liberal) Court leads markets to expect tighter (looser) future fiscal policy.We validate our quasi-experimental setup with sectoral asset price dynamics, such as high-frequency responses of clean energy and health care stocks.Taken together, our findings are consistent with markets interpreting changes in the Supreme Court's ideological composition as news about future fiscal expansions or contractions.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US Supreme Court ideological shifts and their effects on US market expectations for inflation, activity, bond yields and sectoral stocks. The economy studied is the United States, an advanced economy.

title: Estimating the Impact of Targeted Public Policies with Limited Data
abstract: Many public policies aim to support (or change the behavior of) a specific, targeted sub-group of the population.To measure the causal impacts of such policies, social scientists use quasi-experimental methods of policy evaluation, but are often hampered by data availability issues, especially regarding targeted populations, who are often disadvantaged and/or vulnerable.We use power calculations to quantify the challenge of detecting a policy's impact on a small minority population based on population level data, using the impact of abortion bans on economic welfare as an example.We provide insight into this challenge and a roadmap for how researchers can calculate, ex-ante, whether their study is sufficiently powered to detect reasonably meaningful effect sizes.
focus_rationale: The paper is a methodological study on power calculations for policy evaluation, using US abortion bans as an illustrative example rather than focusing on a particular economy's markets.

title: Affirmative Action in Centralized College Admissions Systems
abstract: We study the consequences of affirmative action in college admissions.We develop an empirical framework that distinguishes the effects on marginally benefited and displaced students from the overall effects of the policy.The overall effects include equilibrium reallocations as benefited students leave seats that others fill and displaced students take seats elsewhere, displacing others in turn.We apply this framework to a large-scale policy in Brazil that required all federal institutions to reserve half their seats for racially and socioeconomically disadvantaged applicants.Exploiting admissions cutoffs, we find that marginally benefited targeted students attend and graduate from higher-quality programs.Their graduation gains are about twice the losses of marginally displaced non-targeted students, reflecting targeted students' weaker outside options.To evaluate the overall effects, we estimate a model of degree choices and potential outcomes.Among all reallocated students, benefited students still gain nearly twice what displaced students lose, but equilibrium reallocations make the policy displace about 30%more students than it benefits.Non-targeted students' losses therefore offset about two-thirds of targeted students' graduation gains, leaving a modest net gain across all students.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Brazil's federal college admissions quota policy, a single emerging economy. Its link to markets is weak, covering education outcomes and labour-relevant graduation gains rather than pricing or policy transmission.

title: Strategic Complementarity and Persistence in Linear-Quadratic Mean Field Games
abstract: We study the relation between strategic complementarities and aggregate persistence in linearquadratic mean field games with interactions in states and actions.The framework provides local approximations to common macroeconomic problems, including capital accumulation and multiproduct pricing.We show that the equilibrium aggregate dynamics coincide with those of a single-agent linear-quadratic control problem in which state and action curvatures are adjusted for strategic interactions.This result gives conditions for equilibrium existence, establishes uniqueness, and links strategic interactions to aggregate adjustment.We establish conditions under which stronger state complementarities increase persistence, while stronger action complementarities reduce it, even in multidimensional problems whose underlying matrices are not simultaneously diagonalizable.Under these conditions, internalizing state complementarities makes the utilitarian planner's allocation more persistent, while internalizing action complementarities makes it less persistent.With common shocks, we give conditions under which individual and aggregate dynamics can be combined to identify strategic interactions and model parameters.Finally, we extend the analysis to interactions through higher moments of the state distribution.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical and methodological study of linear-quadratic mean field games with no particular economy as its object; it illustrates with generic macro problems such as capital accumulation and pricing.

title: Measurement Error in Self-Reported Data on Stigmatized Behavior: Experimental Evidence on Intimate Partner Violence
abstract: Error in the measurement of key development outcomes affects our understanding of socioeconomic phenomena and their policy implications.This paper focuses on measuring intimate partner violence (IPV), a public health issue affecting women globally.We introduce a novel, privacy-enhancing data collection method using a ballot, comparing it to standard survey techniques in which responses are not kept private from enumerators, and list experiments, an approach ensuring complete anonymity.Our findings show that improved privacy yields higher and more accurate IPV reports than both, especially among women with low education.By linking our data with two natural experiments, we demonstrate that the non-random nature of underreporting with standard methods can lead to biased estimates of IPV determinants.
focus_rationale: The paper studies intimate partner violence measurement with survey data from developing-country settings, with no macro or financial angle. Its economies are not specified in the abstract, so the EM classification reflects the development context of the outcome.

title: Gains from Trade in Gun Policy: A Compensation-Based Benchmark
abstract: Policies restricting gun sales face substantial political opposition and constitutional constraints.In this paper, we ask how costly it would be to induce potential hand-gun buyers to choose less lethal alternatives.Pairing stated-choice experiments with a behavioral model of firearm choice, we estimate the payments required to induce substitution away from handguns toward long guns or no gun purchase.We then compare these payments with the resulting mortality benefits.We find substantial gains from trade: many prospective handgun buyers require relatively little compensation to switch and targeted compensation can avert homicides at a social cost well below conventional estimates of the value of a statistical life.The extent to which these gains can be realized through compensation, however, depends on the state's information about which consumers would change their choices and at what price.Without this information, uniform subsidies pay consumers who would choose an alternative anyway and overcompensate those willing to switch for less, sharply increasing government expenditure and reducing the optimal scale of compensation.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US handgun purchasing and firearm policy, a US-only setting. It is applied microeconomics with no direct market or macro link.

title: Industrial Policy via the IPO Market
abstract: This paper studies how China uses access to public equity markets as an instrument of industrial policy.We find that policy-favored status, rather than industry Tobin's Q, predicts IPO activity, in contrast to the United States.The effect is economically large: our estimates imply that favored industries had 287% more IPOs and 148% higher IPO proceeds than non-favored industries over 2002 to 2022.We develop a framework to interpret these findings: the government shapes the number of listing opportunities available across industries, while market forces determine which firms obtain these opportunities based on firm fundamentals.Consistent with our framework, policy favor also predicts a valuation premium which persists after listing.
focus_rationale: The paper studies China's use of IPO market access as industrial policy, comparing it with the United States. The focus is China, an emerging economy.

title: Access to Capital and the IPO Decision: An Analysis of US Private Firms
abstract: We analyze firms' IPO decisions using detailed financial data on US private firms.Firms with higher external capital needs are more likely to go public.Following the IPO, firms increase investment and debt issuance, leaving their leverage ratios un-changed from pre-IPO levels.Finally, newly public firms borrow from an expanded pool of lenders on improved terms, and the within-firm dispersion in banks' private risk assessments declines.Our analysis suggests that firms go public to improve their access to capital, which is facilitated by reduced asymmetric information, and that the benefit extends beyond the IPO itself to new sources of debt.
focus_rationale: The paper studies IPO decisions and financing of US private firms, so it is about an advanced economy. Its link to markets is indirect, through corporate access to equity and debt capital.

title: Road Pricing under Heterogeneity
abstract: Congestion pricing policies are widely debated and critics often argue that toll costs outweigh congestion relief.We show theoretically that welfare gains depend on two forces: the extent of driver heterogeneity-both in preferences and in exposure to highly demanded roads and times of day-and the extent of revenue recycling.We quantify the impact of both forces using data from a large-scale experiment that tracked driving behavior with and without usage-based congestion pricing incentives for nearly 10,000 drivers over two years.Using a model of time-varying traffic equilibrium with heterogeneous drivers and a granular road network, we show that a congestion pricing policy using the experiment's price schedule would raise welfare by as much as adding a new lane to every highway and would raise enough revenue to fully compensate losers.Moreover, the extent of driver heterogeneity entails that optimal prices can improve net welfare with only a small fraction of toll revenue.
focus_rationale: The paper studies congestion pricing using a driver experiment and a traffic equilibrium model with a granular road network, with no specific economy named in the abstract, so it is not tied to either developed or emerging markets.

title: The Impact of Central Bank Stock Purchases: Evidence from Discontinuities in Policy Rules
abstract: We trace the impact of central bank stock purchases by exploiting discontinuities in the Bank of Japan's policy rule, which triggers purchases when stock market index movements fall below a threshold.In normal times, the purchases raise the long-term interest rate while leaving no detectable impact on stock prices.After the introduction of yield curve control, which pegs the long-term yield at 0%, interest rates stop responding and stock prices rise robustly following the purchases.Although these results are inconsistent with the inelastic market hypothesis in its original form, general equilibrium extensions with endogenous interest rates explain our findings.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the Bank of Japan's stock purchase program and its effects on Japanese long-term yields and equity prices, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: Learning About Outgroups: The Impact of Broad Versus Deep Interactions
abstract: We hypothesize that broad contact, involving brief interactions with multiple outgroup members, and deep contact, meaning longer interactions with a single outgroup member, play distinct roles in shaping intergroup relations.We set up a factory in India and recruited Hindu and Muslim men to work in pairs on joint production tasks.We randomly assigned participants to work either with the same ingroup or outgroup partner daily (deep contact), a different outgroup partner each day (broad contact), or to a control group.Deep contact strengthens social and economic ties with the outgroup partner.But only broad contact reduces the majority group's misperceptions about outgroup strangers.Using within-treatment variation in partners' pre-treatment productivity, we show that participants in both arms learn about their partners, but broad participants also generalize these belief updates to strangers.These findings align with a model in which independent sampling promotes learning about outgroups more than prolonged interaction with a single individual does.Nevertheless, neither type of contact changes behavior toward the wider outgroup.
focus_rationale: The paper runs a field experiment in a factory in India with Hindu and Muslim male workers, so it studies India specifically. Its link to markets is weak, centred on intergroup contact and social attitudes rather than pricing or macro outcomes.

title: What Can (and Cannot) Be Learned about Systemic Racial Discrimination from Randomized Controlled Trials?
abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have played a major role in detecting direct forms of racial discrimination.In this essay, we ask whether RCTs can (or cannot) play an equally important role in the case of systemic racial discrimination.We propose a conceptual model of systemic racial discrimination drawing from prior definitions of systemic racism.We then consider a range of possibilities and limitations for how RCTs can help understand systemic racial discrimination, including: (1) the feasibility of manipulating systemic racial discrimination on a large scale; (2) smaller scale approaches; (3) conducting RCTs across different structural settings; (4) the manipulation of the salience of systemic forces; (5) the role of information in reducing systemic racial discrimination; (6) the manipulation of the salience of racial identity; and, finally, (7) examination of strategic responses to systemic racial discrimination.In discussing limitations, we point to other approaches that may fill in the gaps left by RCTs in studying systemic racial discrimination.
focus_rationale: This is a methodological essay on using randomized controlled trials to study systemic racial discrimination, with no specific economy studied. It is not tied to any particular country or market.

title: Does Remote Work Increase Fertility?
abstract: Does working from home increase fertility?I study the 2020 expansion of remote work by comparing changes in births across U.S. college graduates whose majors differed in pre-pandemic teleworkability.Measuring exposure by college major avoids relying on occupations workers may have chosen in response to the expansion.Among married women, a one-standard-deviation increase in teleworkability reduced annual birth rates by 2 percent and increased full-time employment by 1.3 percent.I find no statistically significant effects on fertility among men or unmarried women, or on marriage or divorce.Accounting exercises suggest that increased employment can explain about half of the decline in births.The results suggest that returning to prepandemic telework levels would raise the total fertility rate by 0.09 births per woman.
focus_rationale: The paper studies U.S. college graduates and the 2020 expansion of remote work in the United States, so it is mainly about an advanced economy.

title: When Does Randomized Oversight Align AI Agents That Can Conceal?
abstract: Oversight changes the evidence it relies on.We ask when randomized audits and scoring align AI agents that can conceal misconduct and alter records.Stronger auditing makes undeterred violations better hidden.Because the provider writes the agent's objective, sanctions need not stop at forfeiture, and rare audits deter every type of agent if evidence survives concealment and audit draws cannot be learned in advance.When evidence can be erased, deterrence must come from lower gains from violation, such as credit for stopping, or from costlier or fewer ways to conceal.These conditions identify what failed when agents in OpenAI's cybersecurity evaluations compromised parts of Hugging Face's infrastructure in July 2026.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical study of AI agent oversight and mechanism design with no specific economy studied, so it is Transversal. It references a cybersecurity incident but does not analyze any particular country's markets.

title: Indirect Variational Inference: Applications to Earnings Dynamics
abstract: Latent-variable models are central to economics but often entail intractable integration.Variational inference (VI), widely used in machine learning, turns this integration into tractable, differentiable optimization by replacing the likelihood with a variational objective.However, guarantees of recovering the true parameters remain limited when the variational family is insufficiently flexible -a key obstacle to the adoption of VI in economics.We first evaluate VI in models of earnings dynamics and show that the choice of variational posterior is crucial.We then introduce indirect variational inference (IVI), which treats VI as an auxiliary model and corrects the bias induced by the variational approximation.IVI retains much of VI's tractability because it does not require computing the likelihood.We apply these methods to models allowing for nonlinear persistence, non-Gaussian and serially correlated transitory shocks, and latent heterogeneity.Across simulated and empirical applications, flexible variational families combined with IVI deliver reliable estimates.
focus_rationale: The paper is a methodological contribution on variational inference applied to earnings dynamics models, with simulated and empirical applications not tied to a specific economy's markets. It is not specific to either emerging or advanced economies.

title: Survival versus Scale: The Effects of Critical Access Hospital Designation
abstract: The Critical Access Hospital (CAH) program, established under the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, provides cost-based Medicare reimbursement to small rural hospitals in exchange for limits on inpatient capacity and service scope.We estimate the effects of CAH designation on hospital finances, capacity, and organizational outcomes using a synthetic difference-in-differences design that exploits the staggered 1999-2002 rollout of state-level CAH availability.We find that CAH designation raises operating margins by three to four percentage points, with no change in liquidity or capital investment, as cost-based reimbursement sustains revenue while expenses fall with scale.Designation also reduces inpatient scale, with significant declines in total beds, obstetric capacity, and nursing staff.Emergency department visits also decline meaningfully, while outpatient volume is largely unchanged.At the same time, CAH designation reduces hospital closures, with no meaningful effect on mergers.These results point to a "survival versus scale" tradeoff across hospitals within a state, wherein designation-based subsidies avert closure for a small number of hospitals while inducing widespread inpatient downsizing among the many more hospitals that convert.Because converting hospitals shed more inpatient capacity than averted closures preserve, the program may reduce aggregate rural inpatient capacity even as it keeps hospitals open.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US rural hospitals under the Medicare Critical Access Hospital program, a single advanced economy.

title: El proceso de desapalancamiento de las sociedades no financieras españolas en el período 2007-2024
abstract: Corporate leverage among Spanish non-financial corporations declined markedly between 2007 and 2024. This adjustment exhibits substantial heterogeneity across firms. By identifying, for each firm, its peak leverage level and the subsequent trough in its time series, the analysis characterises this heterogeneity by examining both the intensity of the adjustment and the change in other firm characteristics between these two points.
focus_rationale: The paper studies deleveraging by Spanish non-financial corporations between 2007 and 2024, a euro area periphery economy classified as DM.

title: President Musalem Answers Four Questions about the Fed
abstract: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem discusses the Fed’s structure, his FOMC meeting preparation, monetary policy independence, and an area deserving more awareness.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
focus_rationale: The interview concerns the US Federal Reserve and FOMC monetary policy, which is an advanced-economy focus.

title: SORCE Insights: An Update on AI and the Data Center Buildout
abstract: CORRECT ORDER OF AUTHORS: Isler, Huettner. The Cleveland Fed's Survey of Regional Conditions and Expectations (SORCE) fielded from September 17 through September 24, 2026, included a set of special questions focused on firms' use of artificial intelligence (AI). This question set was last fielded during March 2026 and detailed in SORCE Insights: How Fourth District Firms Are Using AI. In this iteration, firms were also asked to describe their involvement in the data center buildout. This District Data Brief discusses the top-line results from these questions.
focus_rationale: The brief reports a survey of firms in the Federal Reserve's Fourth District, which covers parts of Ohio, Pennsylvania, Kentucky and West Virginia, so it is about the United States only.

title: Consumers' Attention to Monetary Policy: The Importance of Having "Skin in the Game"
authors: Knotek, Edward S.; Pedemonte, Mathieu; Hajdini, Ina; Mitchell, James; Shiroff, Taylor
abstract: Using a five-year survey of over 170,000 US consumers, we provide a novel direct measure of attention to monetary policy and show that the data strongly support the predictions of a rational inattention model. First, attention is incentive-driven: consumers with "skin in the game"—those planning major purchases like homes or cars—are significantly more attentive to monetary policy news. Second, attention varies systematically with interest rate volatility and news supply, exhibiting cyclical patterns around FOMC meetings. Third, marginal effects of volatility and news supply decline with "skin in the game," implying external factors primarily affect low-skin-in-the-game consumers. These findings imply that, when communication is costly and attention is endogenous, optimal central bank communications in our model target consumers who bear the largest welfare losses from information frictions. This targeted communication approach increases aggregate attention to monetary policy, leading to an amplified response of consumption to interest rate changes.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US consumers' attention to Federal Reserve monetary policy and FOMC communication, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
abstract: Oliver Pfäuti and Edson Wu How do high public debt and fiscal uncertainty interact to shape inflation? We develop a model in which firms face uncertainty about both marginal costs and fiscal policy and choose how much information to acquire before setting prices. Higher debt raises steady-state taxes, affecting attention through two opposing forces. While these taxes reduce the profit stakes of mispricing, they make desired prices more sensitive to tax fluctuations, increasing the value of information. The interaction generates a U-shaped relationship between public debt and attention, and therefore between debt and inflation volatility. Using euro-area firm-level expectations data, we document that the passthrough of expected input-cost growth into expected selling-price growth rises systematically with a country's debt-to-GDP ratio, consistent with the model. In the calibrated general-equilibrium model, an increase in debt from 100% to 175% of GDP raises inflation volatility by about 20%, mainly because firms reallocate attention toward fiscal shocks.
focus_rationale: The empirical evidence uses euro-area firm-level expectations data, and the calibrated general-equilibrium model is set up for the same advanced-economy context, so the paper is mainly about DM economies.

title: Are stablecoins and bank deposits substitutes?
abstract: We test whether stablecoins and bank deposits act as substitutes by estimating the semi-elasticity of stablecoin market capitalization with respect to deposit rate changes. Using local projections fit to weekly U.S. data from January 2019 to June 2025, we find that deposit rate increases predict slower stablecoin growth. To address endogeneity, we exploit a nonlinearity in deposit rate pass-through.
focus_rationale: The paper uses weekly U.S. data to study how deposit rate changes affect stablecoin market capitalization, so it is centred on the United States, an advanced economy.

title: The voice as a neurophysiological marker: applications in implicit emotion perception for Neurocash® and cash design
abstract: This paper looks at the potential use of voice analysis within the Neurocash® framework in cash design. It also brings together insights from psychology, psychophysiology, vocal acoustics and artificial intelligence (AI) to provide a broader interdisciplinary perspective.
focus_rationale: The paper is methodological and interdisciplinary, focused on voice analysis and emotion perception for cash design, with no particular economy studied.

title: Bank Regulation Affects Monetary Policy Transmission
authors: Krainer, John; Paul, Pascal; Greenwald, Daniel L.
abstract: How does monetary policy impact banks’ lending behavior when interest rate changes revalue their securities? Detailed supervisory data show that banks with larger losses on securities during the 2022–23 monetary policy tightening cycle extended less credit to firms. This spillover effect was especially strong for securities that were marked to market and not hedged, and for banks required to include unrealized losses in regulatory capital. These conditions lead to larger reductions in corporate debt and investment, increasing monetary policy’s impact on the economy.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
focus_rationale: The paper studies US banks and US firms' credit during the 2022-23 Federal Reserve tightening cycle, so it is mainly about an advanced economy.

title: In Hot Water? The Macroeconomic Impacts of El Niño
abstract: Despite their potentially major impacts, little is known about how El Niño impact the U.S. economy. El Niños are distinct from other commonly studied weather shocks because they are a global phenomenon, unfold over a period of months, can be forecast months in advance, are relatively infrequent, and have very different effects on weather outcomes depending on the time of year and region. These features make traditional analytical methods ill-suited to studying the economic impacts of El Niño events. In this paper I use a new approach to estimating the impulse response functions of El Niños. I find that El Niños pose material upside risk for PCE prices and employment. The longer-run price effects are driven by core services and food prices and depend on whether La Niñas follow El Niños, a very common occurrence. After modest offsetting initial effects, employment increases are widespread in terms of both sectors and states in the year following the El Niño. These results indicate El Niños can have material impacts on the US economy even though it is neither tropical nor agriculturally focused.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
focus_rationale: The paper estimates macroeconomic effects of El Niño on the United States, an advanced economy, examining PCE prices and employment.

title: Cash Transfers in Developing Countries: Local Multipliers, Aggregate Effects, and External Adjustment
authors: Pennings, Steven; Nguyen, Thuy Lan; Miyamoto, Wataru; Mendes, Arthur
abstract: This paper studies the local and aggregate effects of cash transfers in developing countries, and how both change as the cash transfer program scales up. We build a two-region New Keynesian small open economy model and calibrate it to rich pre-treatment microdata from an ongoing cash transfer experiment in Malawi. The model implies a local multiplier on temporary transfers of about one, which depends on price stickiness, the share of liquidity-constrained households, and home bias in consumption. Spillovers to the rest of the country are negative under Malawi’s restricted international capital mobility and parallel exchange rate regimes, as cash transfers appreciate the real exchange rate and reduce exports. Consequently, the aggregate multiplier is less than the local multiplier. As the program scales up, the local multiplier converges toward the aggregate multiplier, so a scaled-up program may have smaller multipliers than micro-level estimates suggest. However, with unrestricted capital mobility, spillovers can be positive, especially under a fixed exchange rate. These results highlight the importance of the macroeconomic policy environment for aggregate multipliers and the effects of scaled-up transfer programs.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
focus_rationale: The paper studies cash transfers in Malawi, a developing economy, using a two-region small open economy model calibrated to Malawi microdata. It is a single-country EM study.

title: Borrow Now, Complain Later: Payday Lending Laws and Spillovers Across Consumer Finance
authors: Roman, Raluca; Ma, Xiaonan (Flora); Routh, Aditi
abstract: Prohibiting payday lending can reduce complaints to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau by 90 percent.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
focus_rationale: The paper studies US payday lending laws and their effects on consumer finance complaints, which is a US-focused analysis.

title: Has the Investment Boom Expanded U.S. Productive Capacity?
abstract: U.S. productive capacity has expanded, but so far almost entirely in one narrow segment: the industries that make computers, communications equipment, and semiconductors, which account for about 3 percent of U.S. manufacturing output. Capacity in the rest of manufacturing remains below its pre-pandemic level. Where the AI build-out presses hardest on domestic suppliers, adjustment is occurring through higher prices and imports rather than broad new U.S. capacity.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
focus_rationale: The paper studies U.S. manufacturing capacity and the AI-related investment boom in the United States, an advanced economy.

title: Utility Cost Pressures and Energy Insecurity Differ by Household Income
abstract: Utility cost pressures are rising, particularly for low-income households, who spend five times more on utilities as a share of income than high-income households do.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
focus_rationale: The paper concerns US households and utility costs, an advanced economy, so it is classified as DM.

title: What – and How – Should We Teach in Principles of Economics?
abstract: About half of U.S. college students in their first economics course never take another one. A literacy-targeted approach focuses on making sure they understand core concepts well.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
focus_rationale: The paper concerns undergraduate economics teaching in the United States, not any market or economy's dynamics.

title: The Decline of Student Visas and Its Implications
abstract: In the last year and a half, the debate over immigration policy centered on undocumented workers in the U.S. Legal immigration, on the contrary, has not faced significant changes that would directly limit the number of new legal immigrants coming into the country. Despite this being true on the aggregate, a specific visa category does seem to show a significant decrease in numbers: the F-1 student visa, which is the primary visa used by full-time international students. As shown in Figure 1a, issuance of nonimmigrant visa has followed a similar aggregate trend in 2025 as in previous years.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US student visa issuance and immigration policy, a US-only topic with only a weak link to markets.

title: A Behavioral Foundation for the Investment Wedge
authors: Lopez, Pierlauro; Singh, Sanjay R.; L'Huillier, Jean-Paul
abstract: Motivated by behavioral evidence, we develop a tractable method for incorporating competition neglect into a general equilibrium firm investment problem. Competition neglect causes firms to systematically underestimate the investment of their competitors. When we introduce competition neglect into a canonical RBC model, this friction acts like an investment wedge that causes over-investment at first, and under-investment later on. In contrast to a model with exogenous investment shocks, these dynamics are accompanied by a realistic variation in equity premia, even in the absence of financial frictions. Investment booms raise stock prices in general equilibrium, predicting periods of low excess returns going forward. The model can generate realistic comovement of real and financial variables.
